    "Why don't ice creams ever get invited to parties?\n\nBecause they always drip when things heat up!"  
    

Notice this line of the code, where we piece together these different
components into a single chain using LCEL:

    
    
    chain = prompt | model | output_parser  
    

The ` | ` symbol is similar to a [ unix pipe operator ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pipeline_\(Unix\)) , which chains together the different components, feeding the output from one component as input into the next component. 

In this chain the user input is passed to the prompt template, then the prompt
template output is passed to the model, then the model output is passed to the
output parser. Let’s take a look at each component individually to really
understand what’s going on.

###  1\. Prompt  ​

` prompt ` is a ` BasePromptTemplate ` , which means it takes in a dictionary
of template variables and produces a ` PromptValue ` . A ` PromptValue ` is a
wrapper around a completed prompt that can be passed to either an ` LLM `
(which takes a string as input) or ` ChatModel ` (which takes a sequence of
messages as input). It can work with either language model type because it
defines logic both for producing ` BaseMessage ` s and for producing a string.

    
    
    prompt_value = prompt.invoke({"topic": "ice cream"})  
    prompt_value  
    
    
    
    ChatPromptValue(messages=[HumanMessage(content='tell me a short joke about ice cream')])  
    
    
    
    prompt_value.to_messages()  
    
    
    
    [HumanMessage(content='tell me a short joke about ice cream')]  
    
    
    
    prompt_value.to_string()  
    
    
    
    'Human: tell me a short joke about ice cream'  
    

###  2\. Model  ​

The ` PromptValue ` is then passed to ` model ` . In this case our ` model `
is a ` ChatModel ` , meaning it will output a ` BaseMessage ` .

    
    
    message = model.invoke(prompt_value)  
    message  
    
    
    
    AIMessage(content="Why don't ice creams ever get invited to parties?\n\nBecause they always bring a melt down!")

## Parameters `[in, optional] hWnd` Type: **HWND** A handle to the window that will receive WM\_HOTKEY messages generated by the hot key. If this parameter is **NULL**, **WM\_HOTKEY** messages are posted to the message queue of the calling thread and must be processed in the message loop. `[in] id` Type: **int** The identifier of the hot key. If the _hWnd_ parameter is NULL, then the hot key is associated with the current thread rather than with a particular window. If a hot key already exists with the same _hWnd_ and _id_ parameters, see Remarks for the action taken. `[in] fsModifiers` Type: **UINT** The keys that must be pressed in combination with the key specified by the _vk_ parameter in order to generate the WM\_HOTKEY message. The _fsModifiers_ parameter can be a combination of the following values. Expand table | **Value** | **Meaning** | | --- | --- | | **MOD\_ALT**
0x0001 | Either ALT key must be held down. | | **MOD\_CONTROL**
0x0002 | Either CTRL key must be held down. | | **MOD\_NOREPEAT**
0x4000 | Changes the hotkey behavior so that the keyboard auto-repeat does not yield multiple hotkey notifications.
**Windows Vista:** This flag is not supported. | | **MOD\_SHIFT**
0x0004 | Either SHIFT key must be held down. | | **MOD\_WIN**
0x0008 | Either WINDOWS key must be held down. These keys are labeled with the Windows logo. Keyboard shortcuts that involve the WINDOWS key are reserved for use by the operating system. | `[in] vk` Type: **UINT** The virtual-key code of the hot key. See Virtual Key Codes. Section titled: Return value ## Return value Type: **BOOL** If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero. If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call GetLastError. This function fails if you try to associate a hot key with a window created by another thread. Typically, **RegisterHotKey** also fails if the keystrokes specified for the hot key have already been registered for another hot key. However, some pre-existing, default hotkeys registered by the OS (such as PrintScreen, which launches the Snipping tool) may be overridden by another hot key registration when one of the app's windows is in the foreground. Section titled: Remarks ## Remarks When a key is pressed, the system looks for a match against all hot keys. Upon finding a match, the system posts the WM\_HOTKEY message to the message queue of the window with which the hot key is associated. If the hot key is not associated with a window, then the **WM\_HOTKEY** message is posted to the thread associated with the hot key. If a hot key already exists with the same _hWnd_ and _id_ parameters, it is maintained along with the new hot key. The application must explicitly call UnregisterHotKey to unregister the old hot key. The F12 key is reserved for use by the debugger at all times, so it should not be registered as a hot key. Even when you are not debugging an application, F12 is reserved in case a kernel-mode debugger or a just-in-time debugger is resident. An application must specify an id value in the range 0x0000 through 0xBFFF. A shared DLL must specify a value in the range 0xC000 through 0xFFFF (the range returned by the GlobalAddAtom function). To avoid conflicts with hot-key identifiers defined by other shared DLLs, a DLL should use the **GlobalAddAtom** function to obtain the hot-key identifier. \*\*Windows Server 2003: \*\*If a hot key already exists with the same _hWnd_ and _id_ parameters, it is replaced by the new hot key. Section titled: Examples ### Examples The following example shows how to use the **RegisterHotKey** function with the **MOD\_NOREPEAT** flag. In this example, the hotkey 'ALT+b' is registered for the main thread. When the hotkey is pressed, the thread will receive a WM\_HOTKEY message, which will get picked up in the GetMessage call. Because this example uses **MOD\_ALT** with the **MOD\_NOREPEAT** value for _fsModifiers_, the thread will only receive another **WM\_HOTKEY** message when the 'b' key is released and then pressed again while the 'ALT' key is being pressed down. #  sprintf: Use C-style String Formatting Commands

##  Description

A wrapper for the C function ` sprintf ` , that returns a character vector
containing a formatted combination of text and variable values.

##  Usage

    
    
    sprintf(fmt, …)
    gettextf(fmt, …, domain = NULL)

##  Arguments

fmt

a character vector of format strings, each of up to 8192 bytes.

…

values to be passed into ` fmt ` . Only logical, integer, real and character
vectors are supported, but some coercion will be done: see the ‘Details’
section. Up to 100.

domain

see ` [ gettext ](/link/gettext?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` .

##  Value

A character vector of length that of the longest input. If any element of `
fmt ` or any character argument is declared as UTF-8, the element of the
result will be in UTF-8 and have the encoding declared as UTF-8. Otherwise it
will be in the current locale's encoding.

##  Warning

The format string is passed down the OS's ` sprintf ` function, and incorrect
formats can cause the latter to crash the  R  process .  R  does perform
sanity checks on the format, but not all possible user errors on all platforms
have been tested, and some might be terminal.

The behaviour on inputs not documented here is ‘undefined’, which means it is
allowed to differ by platform.

##  Details

` sprintf ` is a wrapper for the system ` sprintf ` C-library function.
Attempts are made to check that the mode of the values passed match the format
supplied, and  R  's special values ( ` NA ` , ` Inf ` , ` -Inf ` and ` NaN `
) are handled correctly.

` gettextf ` is a convenience function which provides C-style string
formatting with possible translation of the format string.

The arguments (including ` fmt ` ) are recycled if possible a whole number of
times to the length of the longest, and then the formatting is done in
parallel. Zero-length arguments are allowed and will give a zero-length
result. All arguments are evaluated even if unused, and hence some types
(e.g., ` "symbol" ` or ` "language" ` , see ` [ typeof
](/link/typeof?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` ) are not allowed.

The following is abstracted from Kernighan and Ritchie (see References):
however the actual implementation will follow the C99 standard and fine
details (especially the behaviour under user error) may depend on the
platform.

The string ` fmt ` contains normal characters, which are passed through to the
output string, and also conversion specifications which operate on the
arguments provided through ` … ` . The allowed conversion specifications start
with a ` % ` and end with one of the letters in the set ` aAdifeEgGosxX% ` .
These letters denote the following types:

` d ` , ` i ` , ` o ` , ` x ` , ` X `

    

Integer value, ` o ` being octal, ` x ` and ` X ` being hexadecimal (using the
same case for ` a-f ` as the code). Numeric variables with exactly integer
values will be coerced to integer. Formats ` d ` and ` i ` can also be used
for logical variables, which will be converted to ` 0 ` , ` 1 ` or ` NA ` .

` f `

    

Double precision value, in “ **f** ixed point” decimal notation of the form
"[-]mmm.ddd". The number of decimal places ("d") is specified by the
precision: the default is 6; a precision of 0 suppresses the decimal point.
Non-finite values are converted to ` NA ` , ` NaN ` or (perhaps a sign
followed by) ` Inf ` .

` e ` , ` E `

    

Double precision value, in “ **e** xponential” decimal notation of the form `
[-]m.ddde[+-]xx ` or ` [-]m.dddE[+-]xx ` .

` g ` , ` G `

    

Double precision value, in ` %e ` or ` %E ` format if the exponent is less
than -4 or greater than or equal to the precision, and ` %f ` format
otherwise. (The precision (default 6) specifies the number of _significant_

##  3.6. Capturing timelapse sequences  ¶

The simplest way to capture long time-lapse sequences is with the [ `
capture_continuous()  ` ](api_camera.html#picamera.PiCamera.capture_continuous
"picamera.PiCamera.capture_continuous") method. With this method, the camera
captures images continually until you tell it to stop. Images are
automatically given unique names and you can easily control the delay between
captures. The following example shows how to capture images with a 5 minute
delay between each shot:

    
    
    from time import sleep
    from picamera import PiCamera
    
    camera = PiCamera()
    camera.start_preview()
    sleep(2)
    for filename in camera.capture_continuous('img{counter:03d}.jpg'):
        print('Captured %s' % filename)
        sleep(300) # wait 5 minutes
    

However, you may wish to capture images at a particular time, say at the start
of every hour. This simply requires a refinement of the delay in the loop (the
[ ` datetime  ` ](https://docs.python.org/3.4/library/datetime.html#module-
datetime "\(in Python v3.4\)") module is slightly easier to use for
calculating dates and times; this example also demonstrates the ` timestamp  `
template in the captured filenames):

    
    
    from time import sleep
    from picamera import PiCamera
    from datetime import datetime, timedelta
    
    def wait():
        # Calculate the delay to the start of the next hour
        next_hour = (datetime.now() + timedelta(hour=1)).replace(
            minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)
        delay = (next_hour - datetime.now()).seconds
        sleep(delay)
    
    camera = PiCamera()
    camera.start_preview()
    wait()
    for filename in camera.capture_continuous('img{timestamp:%Y-%m-%d-%H-%M}.jpg'):
        print('Captured %s' % filename)
        wait()

Each of Series or DataFrame have a ` get  ` method which can return a default

    In [311]: s.get('a')  # equivalent to s['a']

##  Looking up values by index/column labels  #

Sometimes you want to extract a set of values given a sequence of row labels
and column labels, this can be achieved by ` pandas.factorize  ` and NumPy
indexing. For instance:

    
    
    In [313]: df = pd.DataFrame({'col': ["A", "A", "B", "B"],
       .....:                    'A': [80, 23, np.nan, 22],
       .....:                    'B': [80, 55, 76, 67]})
       .....: 
    
    In [314]: df
    Out[314]: 
      col     A   B
    0   A  80.0  80
    1   A  23.0  55
    2   B   NaN  76
    3   B  22.0  67
    
    In [315]: idx, cols = pd.factorize(df['col'])
    
    In [316]: df.reindex(cols, axis=1).to_numpy()[np.arange(len(df)), idx]
    Out[316]: array([80., 23., 76., 67.])
    

Formerly this could be achieved with the dedicated ` DataFrame.lookup  `
method which was deprecated in version 1.2.0 and removed in version 2.0.0.

##  Index objects  #

The pandas [ ` Index  ` ](../reference/api/pandas.Index.html#pandas.Index
"pandas.Index") class and its subclasses can be viewed as implementing an
_ordered multiset_ . Duplicates are allowed.

[ ` Index  ` ](../reference/api/pandas.Index.html#pandas.Index "pandas.Index")
also provides the infrastructure necessary for lookups, data alignment, and
reindexing. The easiest way to create an [ ` Index  `
](../reference/api/pandas.Index.html#pandas.Index "pandas.Index") directly is
to pass a ` list  ` or other sequence to [ ` Index  `
](../reference/api/pandas.Index.html#pandas.Index "pandas.Index") :

    
    
    In [317]: index = pd.Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'])
    
    In [318]: index
    Out[318]: Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'], dtype='object')
    
    In [319]: 'd' in index
    Out[319]: True
    

or using numbers:

    
    
    In [320]: index = pd.Index([1, 5, 12])
    
    In [321]: index
    Out[321]: Index([1, 5, 12], dtype='int64')
    
    In [322]: 5 in index
    Out[322]: True
    

If no dtype is given, ` Index  ` tries to infer the dtype from the data. It is
also possible to give an explicit dtype when instantiating an [ ` Index  `
](../reference/api/pandas.Index.html#pandas.Index "pandas.Index") :

    
    
    In [323]: index = pd.Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'], dtype="string")
    
    In [324]: index
    Out[324]: Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'], dtype='string')
    
    In [325]: index = pd.Index([1, 5, 12], dtype="int8")
    
    In [326]: index
    Out[326]: Index([1, 5, 12], dtype='int8')
    
    In [327]: index = pd.Index([1, 5, 12], dtype="float32")
    
    In [328]: index
    Out[328]: Index([1.0, 5.0, 12.0], dtype='float32')
    

You can also pass a ` name  ` to be stored in the index:

    
    
    In [329]: index = pd.Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'], name='something')
    
    In [330]: index.name
    Out[330]: 'something'
    

The name, if set, will be shown in the console display:

# Mastering Piping Operators in the Unix Command Line: Best Practices for Efficient Command Chaining

One of the most powerful features in the Unix command line is the ability to chain commands together using the piping operator (`|`). This simple symbol allows the output of one command to become the input of another, enabling complex workflows to be constructed from small, modular tools. By mastering piping techniques, you can transform your command-line usage into a highly efficient, streamlined process.

## Understanding the Basics of Piping

At its core, a pipe connects the standard output (stdout) of one process to the standard input (stdin) of another. For example:

```bash
ls -l | grep ".txt"
```

Here, `ls -l` produces a list of files with detailed information, and `grep ".txt"` filters that list to only show entries containing `.txt`. The pipe allows these two commands to communicate directly without temporary files or manual intervention.

The beauty of pipes lies in their composability. Each command in the chain does one thing well, and together they form a powerful toolset. This aligns perfectly with the Unix philosophy: *Write programs that do one thing and do it well.*

## Structuring Command Chains

When constructing a pipeline, think of it as a sequence of data transformations. The first command generates raw output, subsequent commands refine or reshape it, and the final command produces the desired result. For example:

```bash
cat access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
```

- `cat access.log` reads the log file.
- `awk '{print $1}'` extracts the first column (e.g., IP addresses).
- `sort` orders the addresses.
- `uniq -c` counts occurrences.
- `sort -nr` sorts numerically in reverse order, showing most frequent first.

This structured approach makes pipelines easier to read, debug, and maintain.

## Managing Input and Output Streams

Pipes work with standard streams, but sometimes you'll need to redirect or manipulate them for more control. Key techniques include:

- **Redirecting output to a file**:  
  ```bash
  command1 | command2 > result.txt
  ```
  This saves the final output to `result.txt`.

- **Redirecting errors**:  
  ```bash
  command1 2> errors.log
  ```
  This captures standard error (stderr) separately from stdout.

- **Combining stdout and stderr**:  
  ```bash
  command1 2>&1 | command2
  ```
  This merges both streams for further processing.

Understanding these redirection operators is essential when building robust pipelines that handle both expected output and potential error messages.

## Using `tee` for Intermediate Output

Sometimes you want to inspect intermediate results without breaking the pipeline. The `tee` command reads from stdin and writes to stdout *and* a file simultaneously:

```bash
cat data.txt | tee backup.txt | grep "keyword"
```

This duplicates the data stream, allowing you to save it to `backup.txt` while continuing to process it through `grep`.

## Avoiding Common Pitfalls

While piping is powerful, certain practices can prevent errors and inefficiencies:

1. **Minimize unnecessary commands**:  
   Avoid redundant `cat` usage when a command can read a file directly.  
   ```bash
   grep "keyword" file.txt   # more efficient than cat file.txt | grep "keyword"
   ```

2. **Be mindful of buffering**:  
   Some commands buffer output, which can delay data in a pipeline. Use options like `--line-buffered` in `grep` or `awk` when needed.

3. **Test incrementally**:  
   Build pipelines step by step, testing each stage before adding the next. This makes troubleshooting easier.

4. **Document complex chains**:  
   For long pipelines, include comments in scripts or break them into logical segments for clarity.

## Advanced Chaining with Subshells and Process Substitution

For more sophisticated workflows, subshells and process substitution can be combined with pipes:

- **Subshell grouping**:  
  ```bash
  (command1 | command2) | command3
  ```
  This treats the grouped commands as a single unit in the pipeline.

- **Process substitution**:  
  ```bash
  diff <(sort file1) <(sort file2)
  ```
  This allows commands to produce virtual files on the fly for comparison.

These techniques expand the expressive power of the Unix command line, enabling creative solutions to complex problems.

---

Piping operators are a cornerstone of Unix command-line efficiency. By chaining commands thoughtfully, managing streams carefully, and applying best practices, you can harness the full potential of this simple yet transformative feature. Whether you are parsing logs, transforming datasets, or orchestrating complex scripts, mastering pipes will elevate your workflow to a new level of productivity.

# Dynamically Modifying Tkinter Widgets with `setattr` in Python

When building interactive desktop applications with Tkinter, one of the most powerful features you can leverage is Python’s dynamic nature. The ability to change object attributes at runtime opens up a range of possibilities, from updating user interface elements based on live data, to altering event callbacks without restarting the application. In this post, we’ll explore how the built‑in `setattr` function can be applied to Tkinter widget objects to dynamically modify their properties, such as label text, button states, and callback functions.

## Understanding `setattr` in the Context of Tkinter

The `setattr` function in Python allows you to assign a value to an attribute of an object, where the attribute name is provided as a string:

```python
setattr(obj, attribute_name, value)
```

Tkinter’s widgets—like `Label`, `Button`, `Entry`, and so forth—are Python objects whose state is managed through attributes and methods. Many widget properties can be changed simply by calling their dedicated methods (e.g., `label.config(text="New Text")`), but there are situations where `setattr` provides a more generic or dynamic approach, particularly when the attribute name is determined at runtime.

## Changing Label Text Dynamically

Consider a `Label` widget that needs to display different messages based on user actions or background computations. Instead of hardcoding property changes, you can store the attribute name in a variable and use `setattr`:

```python
import tkinter as tk

root = tk.Tk()
status_label = tk.Label(root, text="Ready")
status_label.pack()

# Change text dynamically
attr_to_change = 'text'
new_text = "Processing..."
setattr(status_label, attr_to_change, new_text)

root.mainloop()
```

In this example, the label’s `text` attribute is updated before the main loop runs, but you can just as easily invoke `setattr` from inside an event handler or after receiving data from a network request.

## Modifying Button States at Runtime

Buttons in Tkinter have a `state` attribute that can be `'normal'`, `'disabled'`, or `'active'`. You might want to disable a button while a task is running, and re‑enable it when the task completes:

```python
action_button = tk.Button(root, text="Start Task", command=lambda: print("Task started"))
action_button.pack()

# Disable the button
setattr(action_button, 'state', 'disabled')

# Later on, re-enable it
setattr(action_button, 'state', 'normal')
```

By using `setattr`, you can write code that generically updates any widget’s state without explicitly calling `config` or writing repetitive conditional logic.

## Updating Callback Functions

One of the most interesting applications of `setattr` is changing a widget’s callback function at runtime. The `command` attribute of a `Button` determines what function is called when the button is clicked. You can replace this function dynamically:

```python
def initial_action():
    print("Initial action executed.")

def new_action():
    print("New action executed.")

dynamic_button = tk.Button(root, text="Click Me", command=initial_action)
dynamic_button.pack()

# Swap the callback
setattr(dynamic_button, 'command', new_action)
```

This technique allows you to rewire parts of your UI based on application state. For example, a “Submit” button could become a “Retry” button after a failed network request, simply by changing its `command` attribute.

## Considerations and Best Practices

While `setattr` is flexible, it’s important to remember:

- Not all widget behavior is controlled by simple attributes. Some actions may require calling methods rather than setting attributes directly.
- For Tkinter widgets, many properties are managed internally and exposed via configuration options. Changing certain attributes with `setattr` may not trigger the visual update you expect unless the widget is designed to respond to that attribute change.
- Using `setattr` with dynamically determined attribute names can make code harder to read. Reserve this approach for scenarios where flexibility outweighs clarity.

## Conclusion

Python’s `setattr` function is a powerful tool for dynamically modifying Tkinter widget objects at runtime. Whether you’re changing the text of a label, toggling the state of a button, or swapping out callback functions, `setattr` enables a level of adaptability that can make your GUI applications more responsive and interactive. By understanding which attributes can be safely changed and how Tkinter reacts to these changes, you can build user interfaces that evolve seamlessly as your application runs.

#  Sys.sleep: Suspend Execution for a Time Interval

##  Description

Suspend execution of  R  expressions for a specified time interval.

##  Usage

    
    
    Sys.sleep(time)

##  Arguments

time

The time interval to suspend execution for, in seconds.

##  Value

Invisible ` NULL ` .

##  Details

Using this function allows  R  to temporarily be given very low priority and
hence not to interfere with more important foreground tasks. A typical use is
to allow a process launched from  R  to set itself up and read its input files
before  R  execution is resumed.

The intention is that this function suspends execution of  R  expressions but
wakes the process up often enough to respond to GUI events, typically every
half second. It can be interrupted (e.g.by  Ctrl-C  or  Esc  at the  R
console).

There is no guarantee that the process will sleep for the whole of the
specified interval (sleep might be interrupted), and it may well take slightly
longer in real time to resume execution.

` time ` must be non-negative (and not ` NA ` nor ` NaN ` ): ` Inf ` is
allowed (and might be appropriate if the intention is to wait indefinitely for
an interrupt). The resolution of the time interval is system-dependent, but
will normally be 20ms or better. (On modern Unix-alikes it will be better than
1ms.)

##  Examples

[ Run this code
](https://app.datacamp.com/workspace/preview?_tag=rdocs&rdocsPath=packages%2Fbase%2Fversions%2F3.6.2%2Ftopics%2FSys.sleep&utm_source=r-docs&utm_medium=docs&utm_term=Sys.sleep&utm_content=run_example_in_workspace)

    
    
    # NOT RUN {
    testit <- function(x)
    {
        p1 <- proc.time()
        Sys.sleep(x)
        proc.time() - p1 # The cpu usage should be negligible
    }
    testit(3.7)
    # }

` --generate-cli-skeleton  ` (string) Prints a JSON skeleton to standard

--cli-input-json  ` . Similarly, if provided ` yaml-input  ` it will print a

US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array) instances returns the
index of the first element in an array that satisfies the provided testing
function. If no elements satisfy the testing function, -1 is returned.

See also the [ ` find() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/find) method, which
returns the first element that satisfies the testing function (rather than its
index).

##  Try it

##  Syntax

js

    
    
    findIndex(callbackFn)
    findIndex(callbackFn, thisArg)
    

###  Parameters

` callbackFn `

    

A function to execute for each element in the array. It should return a [
truthy ](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Truthy) value to indicate a matching element has
been found, and a [ falsy ](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Falsy) value otherwise. The
function is called with the following arguments:

` element `

    

The current element being processed in the array.

` index `

    

The index of the current element being processed in the array.

` array `

    

The array ` findIndex() ` was called upon.

` thisArg ` Optional

    

A value to use as ` this ` when executing ` callbackFn ` . See [ iterative
methods ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array#iterative_methods) .

###  Return value

The index of the first element in the array that passes the test. Otherwise, `
-1 ` .

##  Description

The ` findIndex() ` is an [ iterative method ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array#iterative_methods) . It
calls a provided ` callbackFn ` function once for each element in an array in
ascending-index order, until ` callbackFn ` returns a [ truthy ](/en-
US/docs/Glossary/Truthy) value. ` findIndex() ` then returns the index of that
element and stops iterating through the array. If ` callbackFn ` never returns
a truthy value, ` findIndex() ` returns ` -1 ` . Read the [ iterative methods
](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array#iterative_methods)
section for more information about how these methods work in general.

` callbackFn ` is invoked for _every_ index of the array, not just those with
assigned values. Empty slots in [ sparse arrays ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Indexed_collections#sparse_arrays) behave the
same as ` undefined ` .

The ` findIndex() ` method is [ generic ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array#generic_array_methods) .
It only expects the ` this ` value to have a ` length ` property and integer-
keyed properties.

##  Examples

###  Find the index of a prime number in an array

The following example returns the index of the first element in the array that
is a prime number, or ` -1 ` if there is no prime number.

js

    
    
    function isPrime(element) {
      if (element % 2 === 0 || element < 2) {
        return false;
      }
      for (let factor = 3; factor <= Math.sqrt(element); factor += 2) {
        if (element % factor === 0) {
          return false;
        }
      }
      return true;
    }
    
    console.log([4, 6, 8, 9, 12].findIndex(isPrime)); // -1, not found
    console.log([4, 6, 7, 9, 12].findIndex(isPrime)); // 2 (array[2] is 7)
    

###  Using the third argument of callbackFn

The ` array ` argument is useful if you want to access another element in the
array, especially when you don't have an existing variable that refers to the
array. The following example first uses ` filter() ` to extract the positive
values and then uses ` findIndex() ` to find the first element that is less
than its neighbors.

js

    
    
    const numbers = [3, -1, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6];
    const firstTrough = numbers
      .filter((num) => num > 0)
      .findIndex((num, idx, arr) => {
        // Without the arr argument, there's no way to easily access the
        // intermediate array without saving it to a variable.
        if (idx > 0 && num >= arr[idx - 1]) return false;
        if (idx < arr.length - 1 && num >= arr[idx + 1]) return false;
        return true;
      });

#  pandas.DataFrame.plot.box  #

DataFrame.plot.  box  (  _ by  =  None  _ , _ **  kwargs  _ )  [ [source]
](https://github.com/pandas-
dev/pandas/blob/v2.2.2/pandas/plotting/_core.py#L1282-L1347) #

    

Make a box plot of the DataFrame columns.

A box plot is a method for graphically depicting groups of numerical data
through their quartiles. The box extends from the Q1 to Q3 quartile values of
the data, with a line at the median (Q2). The whiskers extend from the edges
of box to show the range of the data. The position of the whiskers is set by
default to 1.5*IQR (IQR = Q3 - Q1) from the edges of the box. Outlier points
are those past the end of the whiskers.

For further details see Wikipediaâs entry for [ boxplot
](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_plot) .

A consideration when using this chart is that the box and the whiskers can
overlap, which is very common when plotting small sets of data.

Parameters  :

    

**by** str or sequence

    

Column in the DataFrame to group by.

Changed in version 1.4.0:  Previously,  by  is silently ignore and makes no
groupings

****kwargs**

    

Additional keywords are documented in [ ` DataFrame.plot()  `
](pandas.DataFrame.plot.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot "pandas.DataFrame.plot") .

#  torch.repeat_interleave  ¶

torch.  repeat_interleave  (  _ input  _ , _ repeats  _ , _ dim  =  None  _ ,
_ *  _ , _ output_size  =  None  _ )  →  [ Tensor
](../tensors.html#torch.Tensor "torch.Tensor") ¶

    

Repeat elements of a tensor.

Warning

This is different from [ ` torch.Tensor.repeat()  `
](torch.Tensor.repeat.html#torch.Tensor.repeat "torch.Tensor.repeat") but
similar to ` numpy.repeat  ` .

Parameters

    

  * **input** ( [ _Tensor_ ](../tensors.html#torch.Tensor "torch.Tensor") ) – the input tensor. 

  * **repeats** ( [ _Tensor_ ](../tensors.html#torch.Tensor "torch.Tensor") _or_ [ _int_ ](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#int "\(in Python v3.12\)") ) – The number of repetitions for each element. repeats is broadcasted to fit the shape of the given axis. 

  * **dim** ( [ _int_ ](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#int "\(in Python v3.12\)") _,_ _optional_ ) – The dimension along which to repeat values. By default, use the flattened input array, and return a flat output array. 

Keyword Arguments

    

**output_size** ( [ _int_
](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#int "\(in Python v3.12\)")
_,_ _optional_ ) – Total output size for the given axis ( e.g. sum of
repeats). If given, it will avoid stream synchronization needed to calculate
output shape of the tensor.

Returns

    

Repeated tensor which has the same shape as input, except along the given
axis.

Return type

    

[ Tensor ](../tensors.html#torch.Tensor "torch.Tensor")

Example:

    
    
    >>> x = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3])
    >>> x.repeat_interleave(2)
    tensor([1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3])
    >>> y = torch.tensor([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
    >>> torch.repeat_interleave(y, 2)
    tensor([1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4])
    >>> torch.repeat_interleave(y, 3, dim=1)
    tensor([[1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2],
            [3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4]])
    >>> torch.repeat_interleave(y, torch.tensor([1, 2]), dim=0)
    tensor([[1, 2],
            [3, 4],
            [3, 4]])
    >>> torch.repeat_interleave(y, torch.tensor([1, 2]), dim=0, output_size=3)
    tensor([[1, 2],
            [3, 4],
            [3, 4]])
    

If the  repeats  is  tensor([n1, n2, n3, …])  , then the output will be
tensor([0, 0, …, 1, 1, …, 2, 2, …, …])  where  0  appears  n1  times,  1
appears  n2  times,  2  appears  n3  times, etc.

    tensor([0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2])

Examples

**Series**

    
    
    >>> s = pd.Series([2, np.nan, 5, -1, 0])
    >>> s
    0    2.0
    1    NaN
    2    5.0
    3   -1.0
    4    0.0
    dtype: float64
    

By default, NA values are ignored.

    
    
    >>> s.cummax()
    0    2.0
    1    NaN
    2    5.0
    3    5.0
    4    5.0
    dtype: float64
    

To include NA values in the operation, use ` skipna=False  `

    
    
    >>> s.cummax(skipna=False)
    0    2.0
    1    NaN
    2    NaN
    3    NaN
    4    NaN
    dtype: float64
    

**DataFrame**

    
    
    >>> df = pd.DataFrame([[2.0, 1.0],
    ...                    [3.0, np.nan],
    ...                    [1.0, 0.0]],
    ...                   columns=list('AB'))
    >>> df
         A    B
    0  2.0  1.0
    1  3.0  NaN
    2  1.0  0.0
    

By default, iterates over rows and finds the maximum in each column. This is
equivalent to ` axis=None  ` or ` axis='index'  ` .

    
    
    >>> df.cummax()
         A    B
    0  2.0  1.0
    1  3.0  NaN
    2  3.0  1.0
    

To iterate over columns and find the maximum in each row, use ` axis=1  `

    
    
    >>> df.cummax(axis=1)
         A    B
    0  2.0  2.0
    1  3.0  NaN
    2  1.0  1.0

32 bits will be converted to a 32-bit integer:

    
    
    Before: 11100110111110100000000000000110000000000001
    After:              10100000000000000110000000000001
    

The right operand will be converted to an unsigned 32-bit integer and then
taken modulo 32, so the actual shift offset will always be a positive integer
between 0 and 31, inclusive. For example, ` 100 >>> 32 ` is the same as ` 100
>>> 0 ` (and produces ` 100 ` ) because 32 modulo 32 is 0.

##  Examples

###  Using unsigned right shift

js

    
    
    9 >>> 2; // 2
    -9 >>> 2; // 1073741821
    

Unsigned right shift doesn't work with BigInts.

js

    
    
    9n >>> 2n; // TypeError: BigInts have no unsigned right shift, use >> instead

#  Choosing the runner for a job

Define the type of machine that will process a job in your workflow.

##  Overview

Use ` jobs.<job_id>.runs-on ` to define the type of machine to run the job on.

  * The destination machine can be either a  GitHub-hosted runner  ,  larger runner  , or a  self-hosted runner  . 

  * You can target runners based on the labels assigned to them, or their group membership, or a combination of these. 

  * You can provide ` runs-on ` as: 

    * a single string 
    * a single variable containing a string 
    * an array of strings, variables containing strings, or a combination of both 
    * a ` key: value ` pair using the ` group ` or ` labels ` keys 
  * If you specify an array of strings or variables, your workflow will execute on any runner that matches all of the specified ` runs-on ` values. For example, here the job will only run on a self-hosted runner that has the labels ` linux ` , ` x64 ` , and ` gpu ` : 
    
        runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, x64, gpu]
    

For more information, see "  Choosing self-hosted runners  ."

  * You can mix strings and variables in an array. For example: 
    
        on:
      workflow_dispatch:
        inputs:
          chosen-os:
            required: true
            type: choice
            options:
            - Ubuntu
            - macOS
    
    jobs:
      test:
        runs-on: [self-hosted, "${{ inputs.chosen-os }}"]
        steps:
        - run: echo Hello world!
    

  * If you would like to run your workflow on multiple machines, use [ ` jobs.<job_id>.strategy ` ](/en/actions/using-workflows/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions#jobsjob_idstrategy) . 

**Note:** Quotation marks are not required around simple strings like ` self-
hosted ` , but they are required for expressions like ` "${{ inputs.chosen-os
}}" ` .

###  Choosing GitHub-hosted runners

If you use a GitHub-hosted runner, each job runs in a fresh instance of a
runner image specified by ` runs-on ` .

Available GitHub-hosted runner labels are:

**OS (YAML workflow label)** |  **Notes**  
---|---  
` ubuntu-latest ` , ` ubuntu-22.04 ` , ` ubuntu-20.04 ` |  The ` ubuntu-latest ` label currently uses the Ubuntu 22.04 runner image.

](functions.html#hasattr "hasattr") call, or raise an [ ` AttributeError  `
](exceptions.html#AttributeError "AttributeError") when an attribute is
fetched. You can do this by providing an object as a ` spec  ` for a mock, but
that isnât always convenient.

You âblockâ attributes by deleting them. Once deleted, accessing an
attribute will raise an [ ` AttributeError  ` ](exceptions.html#AttributeError
"AttributeError") .

    
    
    >>> mock = MagicMock()
    >>> hasattr(mock, 'm')
    True
    >>> del mock.m
    >>> hasattr(mock, 'm')
    False
    >>> del mock.f
    >>> mock.f
    Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
    AttributeError: f

Since ânameâ is an argument to the  ` Mock  ` constructor, if you want
your mock object to have a ânameâ attribute you canât just pass it in at
creation time. There are two alternatives. One option is to use  `
configure_mock()  ` :

    
    
    >>> mock = MagicMock()
    >>> mock.configure_mock(name='my_name')
    >>> mock.name
    'my_name'
    

A simpler option is to simply set the ânameâ attribute after mock
creation:

    
    
    >>> mock = MagicMock()
    >>> mock.name = "foo"
    

###  Attaching Mocks as Attributes  Â¶

When you attach a mock as an attribute of another mock (or as the return
value) it becomes a âchildâ of that mock. Calls to the child are recorded
in the  ` method_calls  ` and  ` mock_calls  ` attributes of the parent. This
is useful for configuring child mocks and then attaching them to the parent,
or for attaching mocks to a parent that records all calls to the children and
allows you to make assertions about the order of calls between mocks:

    
    
    >>> parent = MagicMock()
    >>> child1 = MagicMock(return_value=None)
    >>> child2 = MagicMock(return_value=None)
    >>> parent.child1 = child1
    >>> parent.child2 = child2
    >>> child1(1)
    >>> child2(2)
    >>> parent.mock_calls
    [call.child1(1), call.child2(2)]
    

The exception to this is if the mock has a name. This allows you to prevent
the âparentingâ if for some reason you donât want it to happen.

    
    
    >>> mock = MagicMock()
    >>> not_a_child = MagicMock(name='not-a-child')
    >>> mock.attribute = not_a_child
    >>> mock.attribute()
    <MagicMock name='not-a-child()' id='...'>
    >>> mock.mock_calls
    []

####  8.3.3 Working with fields

Use  -1  ,  -2  to set the key fields for each of the input files. Ensure the
preceding ` sort ` commands operated on the same fields.

The following example joins two files, using the values from seventh field of
the first file and the third field of the second file:

    
    
    $ sort -k 7b,7 file1 > file1.sorted
    $ sort -k 3b,3 file2 > file2.sorted
    $ join -1 7 -2 3 file1.sorted file2.sorted > file3
    

If the field number is the same for both files, use  -j  :

    
    
    $ sort -k4b,4 file1 > file1.sorted
    $ sort -k4b,4 file2 > file2.sorted
    $ join -j4    file1.sorted file2.sorted > file3
    

Both ` sort ` and ` join ` operate of whitespace-delimited fields. To specify
a different delimiter, use  -t  in _both_ :

    
    
    $ sort -t, -k3b,3 file1 > file1.sorted
    $ sort -t, -k3b,3 file2 > file2.sorted
    $ join -t, -j3    file1.sorted file2.sorted > file3
    

To specify a tab (  ASCII  0x09) character instead of whitespace, use:  2

    
    
    $ sort -t$'\t' -k3b,3 file1 > file1.sorted
    $ sort -t$'\t' -k3b,3 file2 > file2.sorted
    $ join -t$'\t' -j3    file1.sorted file2.sorted > file3
    

If ‘  join -t ''  ’ is specified then the whole line is considered which
matches the default operation of sort:

    
    
    $ sort file1 > file1.sorted
    $ sort file2 > file2.sorted
    $ join -t '' file1.sorted file2.sorted > file3
    

* * *

literal tab.

#  lower.tri: Lower and Upper Triangular Part of a Matrix

##  Description

Returns a matrix of logicals the same size of a given matrix with entries `
TRUE ` in the lower or upper triangle.

##  Usage

    
    
    lower.tri(x, diag = FALSE)
    upper.tri(x, diag = FALSE)

##  Arguments

x

a matrix or other  R  object with ` length(dim(x)) == 2 ` . For back
compatibility reasons, when the above is not fulfilled, ` [ as.matrix
](/link/as.matrix?package=base&version=3.6.2) (x) ` is called first.

diag

logical. Should the diagonal be included?

` [ diag ](/link/diag?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` , ` [ matrix
](/link/matrix?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` ; further ` [ row
](/link/row?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` and ` [ col
](/link/col?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` on which ` lower.tri() ` and `
upper.tri() ` are built.

# Optimizing Console Output in High-Performance Node.js Applications

In modern Node.js development, console output is more than just a debugging tool — it’s often a critical part of application observability, diagnostics, and performance monitoring. As applications scale, naive logging practices can become a bottleneck, impacting throughput and latency. This post explores advanced techniques to optimize console output, covering efficient logging libraries, asynchronous output strategies, and integrating logs into monitoring systems.

---

## The Performance Cost of Logging

Node.js executes JavaScript on a single-threaded event loop. While asynchronous I/O operations allow concurrent handling of requests, synchronous console output can block the event loop. Using `console.log` extensively in high-traffic services can lead to noticeable slowdowns, especially when printing large data sets or frequent log messages. Each log call involves formatting, writing to `stdout`, and flushing the output buffer — all potentially expensive operations under load.

---

## Leveraging Logging Libraries

Rather than relying solely on the built-in `console` methods, specialized logging libraries offer performance and feature advantages:

- **Winston**  
  A popular, extensible logging library supporting multiple transports (console, files, databases, HTTP endpoints). Winston allows fine-grained log levels, structured JSON output, and batching of writes, reducing I/O overhead.

- **Pino**  
  Designed for speed, Pino minimizes log formatting overhead and writes logs as JSON for easy parsing. Benchmarks show Pino significantly outperforming `console.log` under high concurrency.

- **Bunyan**  
  Similar to Pino, Bunyan outputs structured logs and supports streams for flexible processing. Its design allows logs to be piped into external processors without blocking application execution.

When choosing a library, consider not only speed but also compatibility with your monitoring infrastructure and ease of integration.

---

## Asynchronous File and Stream Output

A common optimization is to decouple log generation from log writing. Instead of writing directly to `stdout` or a file synchronously, use asynchronous streams or queues:

- **Write Streams**  
  Create a `fs.createWriteStream` instance and pipe logs into it. This ensures that disk writes do not block the event loop and can be buffered.

- **Message Queues**  
  In distributed systems, send logs to a message broker (e.g., Kafka, RabbitMQ) asynchronously. Downstream consumers can process and store logs without affecting application latency.

- **Batching**  
  Aggregate multiple log messages into a single write operation. This reduces the number of I/O calls and improves throughput.

By separating log production from log persistence, you can maintain responsive request handling even under heavy logging conditions.

---

## Integration with Monitoring and Observability Systems

Optimized logging becomes truly valuable when connected to broader observability pipelines. Tools like Elastic Stack (ELK), Grafana Loki, or AWS CloudWatch can ingest structured logs for visualization, alerting, and analytics.

Key integration practices include:

- **Structured Logging**  
  Use consistent, machine-readable formats (JSON) so logs can be parsed automatically. Include fields like timestamp, log level, request ID, and contextual metadata.

- **Log Levels and Filtering**  
  Control verbosity dynamically. For example, enable `debug` level logs only in development or during incident investigation.

- **Correlation IDs**  
  Tag related log messages with unique identifiers to trace requests across microservices.

- **Centralized Collection**  
  Forward logs to a central service rather than scattering them across instances. Centralization aids in pattern recognition and anomaly detection.

---

## Balancing Detail and Performance

While detailed logs can be invaluable for troubleshooting, excessive logging can degrade performance and overwhelm storage systems. Striking the right balance involves:

- Identifying critical events to log.
- Using sampling for high-frequency events.
- Periodically reviewing log output to remove obsolete or redundant entries.

In high-performance Node.js applications, every millisecond counts. Optimizing console output is not just a matter of aesthetics — it’s a strategic decision that impacts scalability, maintainability, and operational insight.

---

**Conclusion**  
Efficient logging in Node.js requires a deliberate approach: selecting the right tools, adopting asynchronous patterns, and integrating with monitoring systems in a way that preserves application responsiveness. By investing in these techniques, development teams can ensure that their applications remain performant while delivering rich, actionable telemetry for operational excellence.

formly-distributed pseudo-random number in the inclusive range
[ ` _ min  _ ` , ` _ max  _ ` ].

##  Syntax  ¶

    
    
    UNIFORM( <min> , <max> , <gen> )
    

Copy

##  Arguments  ¶

` _ min  _ `

    

A constant specifying the minimum value (inclusive) of the generated number.

` _ max  _ `

    

A constant specifying the maximum value (inclusive) of the generated number.

` _ gen  _ `

    

An expression that serves as a raw source of uniform random numbers, typically
the ` RANDOM  ` function. For more information, see the Data Generation
Functions [ Usage Notes  ](../functions-data-generation.html#label-rand-dist-
functions) .

##  Returns  ¶

If either or both of ` _ min  _ ` or ` _ max  _ ` is a floating-point number,
` UNIFORM  ` returns a floating-point number. If both ` _ min  _ ` and ` _ max
_ ` are integers, ` UNIFORM  ` returns an integer.

##  Usage Notes  ¶

This function is related to, but different from, the [ RANDOM  ](random)
function. Both functions generate uniform distributions, but there are
differences in the ranges of the values returned.

  * ` RANDOM  ` generates pseudo-random 64-bit integers. It accepts an optional seed that allows sequences to be repeated. 

  * ` UNIFORM  ` generates random integer or floating-point numbers in the specified range.

#  511 Network Authentication Required

The HTTP **` 511 Network Authentication Required ` ** response status code
indicates that the client needs to authenticate to gain network access.

This status is not generated by origin servers, but by intercepting proxies
that control access to the network.

Network operators sometimes require some authentication, acceptance of terms,
or other user interaction before granting access (for example in an internet
cafÃ© or at an airport). They often identify clients who have not done so
using their Media Access Control (MAC) addresses.

# Creating Dynamic, User-Friendly Drop-Down Menus in Microsoft Excel

When working with large datasets in Microsoft Excel, drop-down menus are a powerful tool for guiding data entry, enforcing consistency, and reducing errors. However, many users face a common challenge: the values that drive the logic of their spreadsheets—such as internal codes, IDs, or abbreviated labels—are not always intuitive for end-users. The solution lies in customizing drop-down menus to display user-friendly names while still referencing the underlying codes for calculations and lookups. This article walks through how to achieve this by linking drop-down lists to dynamic named ranges.

---

## Understanding the Problem

In many spreadsheet designs, the underlying data is stored in a structured table containing multiple columns. One column might hold internal codes (e.g., product IDs, department codes), while another contains human-readable names. While internal codes are essential for formulas, pivot tables, and database integration, they are not ideal for manual selection in a drop-down list. A more intuitive approach is to present the friendly name to the user, while Excel stores the corresponding code behind the scenes.

---

## Step 1: Organize Your Source Data

Begin by arranging your source data in a clear tabular format. For example:

| Product Code | Product Name       |
|--------------|--------------------|
| P001         | Deluxe Coffee Mug  |
| P002         | Stainless Steel Flask |
| P003         | Ceramic Tea Pot    |

Place this table on a dedicated worksheet, such as `LookupData`. This separation keeps your working sheets clean and makes maintaining the lookup data easier.

---

## Step 2: Create a Dynamic Named Range

A dynamic named range automatically expands or contracts as you add or remove items from your source list. This ensures that your drop-down menu always reflects the current dataset.

1. Go to **Formulas** → **Name Manager**.
2. Click **New** and assign a descriptive name, such as `ProductNames`.
3. In the “Refers to” box, enter a formula using `OFFSET` or `INDEX` with `COUNTA` to create a dynamic range. For example:

   ```
   =OFFSET(LookupData!$B$2,0,0,COUNTA(LookupData!$B:$B)-1,1)
   ```

   This formula starts at cell `B2` (the first product name) and expands downward based on the number of non-empty cells in column B.

---

## Step 3: Link Codes to Friendly Names

To maintain the relationship between codes and friendly names, create a second named range for the codes:

```
=OFFSET(LookupData!$A$2,0,0,COUNTA(LookupData!$A:$A)-1,1)
```

Name this range `ProductCodes`.

You now have two parallel dynamic ranges: one for display (`ProductNames`) and one for underlying values (`ProductCodes`).

---

## Step 4: Build the Drop-Down Menu

Select the cell or range where you want the drop-down menu. Navigate to **Data** → **Data Validation**. In the Data Validation dialog:

- Set “Allow” to **List**.
- In “Source,” enter `=ProductNames`.

This ensures that the drop-down displays friendly product names. When a user selects an item, the name is stored in the cell.

---

## Step 5: Use Lookups to Retrieve Codes

Since Excel is displaying names in the drop-down, you can use a lookup formula to retrieve the corresponding code for internal processing. For example:

```
=INDEX(ProductCodes, MATCH(SelectedProductName, ProductNames, 0))
```

Here, `SelectedProductName` is the cell containing the chosen friendly name. The `INDEX`/`MATCH` combination finds the matching code from the `ProductCodes` range. This allows you to store or use the internal code without exposing it directly in the user interface.

---

## Step 6: Maintaining and Expanding

The beauty of dynamic named ranges is that you can add new products simply by appending them to your source table. The ranges automatically adjust, and the drop-down list updates without further configuration. This approach scales well for hundreds of items and is particularly useful when working with data imported from external sources.

---

## Conclusion

Customizing Excel drop-down menus to show user-friendly names while retaining internal codes behind the scenes creates a more intuitive and professional spreadsheet. By using dynamic named ranges, you ensure that your lists are always up-to-date, reduce the need for manual maintenance, and bridge the gap between usability and functional accuracy. With this method, your end-users interact with clear, descriptive options, while your formulas and reports continue to run on reliable, structured identifiers.

By default, all modules have a usable repr, however depending on the
attributes set above, and in the moduleâs spec, you can more explicitly
control the repr of module objects.

If the module has a spec ( ` __spec__  ` ), the import machinery will try to
generate a repr from it. If that fails or there is no spec, the import system
will craft a default repr using whatever information is available on the
module. It will try to use the ` module.__name__  ` , ` module.__file__  ` ,
and ` module.__loader__  ` as input into the repr, with defaults for whatever
information is missing.

Here are the exact rules used:

  * If the module has a ` __spec__  ` attribute, the information in the spec is used to generate the repr. The ânameâ, âloaderâ, âoriginâ, and âhas_locationâ attributes are consulted. 

  * If the module has a ` __file__  ` attribute, this is used as part of the moduleâs repr. 

  * If the module has no ` __file__  ` but does have a ` __loader__  ` that is not ` None  ` , then the loaderâs repr is used as part of the moduleâs repr. 

  * Otherwise, just use the moduleâs ` __name__  ` in the repr. 

Changed in version 3.12:  Use of ` module_repr()  ` , having been deprecated

###  5.4.7.  Cached bytecode invalidation  Â¶

Before Python loads cached bytecode from a ` .pyc  ` file, it checks whether
the cache is up-to-date with the source ` .py  ` file. By default, Python does
this by storing the sourceâs last-modified timestamp and size in the cache
file when writing it. At runtime, the import system then validates the cache
file by checking the stored metadata in the cache file against the sourceâs
metadata.

Python also supports âhash-basedâ cache files, which store a hash of the
source fileâs contents rather than its metadata. There are two variants of
hash-based ` .pyc  ` files: checked and unchecked. For checked hash-based `
.pyc  ` files, Python validates the cache file by hashing the source file and
comparing the resulting hash with the hash in the cache file. If a checked

a new checked hash-based cache file. For unchecked hash-based ` .pyc  ` files,
Python simply assumes the cache file is valid if it exists. Hash-based ` .pyc
` files validation behavior may be overridden with the [ ` --check-hash-based-
pycs  ` ](../using/cmdline.html#cmdoption-check-hash-based-pycs) flag.

# Optimizing Startup Time in Flask Applications for High-Traffic Sites

When running a Flask-based web application in a high-traffic environment, every millisecond of latency matters. The time it takes for a server to start and be ready to serve requests can directly impact user experience, uptime during deployments, and the ability to handle sudden traffic surges. This post explores practical methods to reduce startup overhead by preloading HTML templates, initializing database connections early, and caching API responses—ensuring that your application delivers responses faster from the moment it comes online.

---

## Preloading HTML Templates

Flask uses Jinja2 for template rendering, and by default, templates are loaded from disk when first used. In a busy application, this lazy-loading behavior can result in noticeable delays during early requests, especially if templates are large or numerous.

A simple optimization is to force template compilation at startup. This can be achieved by iterating through all templates in your `templates` directory and rendering them once during the application initialization phase. Doing so ensures that the Jinja2 environment caches the compiled templates in memory, reducing per-request rendering time for the first users hitting your site after a restart.

Example:

```python
from flask import Flask, render_template
import os

def preload_templates(app):
    template_dir = os.path.join(app.root_path, 'templates')
    for root, _, files in os.walk(template_dir):
        for file in files:
            if file.endswith('.html'):
                path = os.path.relpath(os.path.join(root, file), template_dir)
                render_template(path)

app = Flask(__name__)
with app.app_context():
    preload_templates(app)
```

This approach shifts the cost of template compilation from request time to startup, which is often preferable in production deployments.

---

## Initializing Database Connections

Database connection setup can be surprisingly expensive, particularly if the connection requires authentication, encryption, or complex configuration. Many applications open database connections lazily—only when a request first needs them. This can cause the first few requests after a restart to be slower than subsequent ones.

To mitigate this, initialize database connections during server startup. For example, if using SQLAlchemy, you can create an engine and establish a connection pool before serving any requests. This ensures that the connection overhead is absorbed into the startup phase, and the application can immediately use ready-to-go connections when traffic arrives.

```python
from flask_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemy

db = SQLAlchemy()

def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.config['SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI'] = 'postgresql://user:pass@host/dbname'
    db.init_app(app)
    with app.app_context():
        # Warm up the connection pool
        db.session.execute('SELECT 1')
    return app
```

By priming the connection pool early, you reduce the likelihood of latency spikes during the first few queries.

---

## Caching API Responses

For applications that rely on third-party APIs, response times can vary due to network latency or remote server load. If certain API calls are predictable or repeated often, caching their responses at startup can save valuable time and bandwidth.

Startup caching works best for static or infrequently changing data—such as configuration information, metadata, or reference datasets. You can store this data in memory, a local key-value store like Redis, or even a file-based cache.

Example with in-memory caching:

```python
import requests

api_cache = {}

def preload_api_data():
    endpoints = [
        'https://api.example.com/config',
        'https://api.example.com/countries'
    ]
    for url in endpoints:
        response = requests.get(url)
        api_cache[url] = response.json()

preload_api_data()
```

By preloading and caching these responses, your application can serve them instantly without making repeated external calls during high-traffic periods.

---

## Deployment Considerations

Preloading templates, initializing database connections, and caching API responses all shift work from request-time to startup-time. While this can significantly improve user-facing latency, it’s important to monitor startup duration, especially in environments with strict deployment windows or auto-scaling triggers.

In containerized deployments, for example, longer startup times may delay readiness probes, causing load balancers to route traffic later than expected. Balancing startup preloading with operational constraints is key.

---

## Conclusion

Optimizing startup time in Flask applications is a strategic way to ensure consistent performance for high-traffic sites. By preloading templates, warming up database connections, and caching critical API responses, you can reduce latency for initial requests and improve overall responsiveness. These changes allow the application to be fully prepared to serve content the moment it comes online, enhancing both user experience and operational efficiency.

###  Gradient penalty  ¶

A gradient penalty implementation commonly creates gradients using [ `
torch.autograd.grad()  ` ](../autograd.html#torch.autograd.grad
"torch.autograd.grad") , combines them to create the penalty value, and adds
the penalty value to the loss.

Here’s an ordinary example of an L2 penalty without gradient scaling or
autocasting:

    
    
    for epoch in epochs:
        for input, target in data:
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            output = model(input)
            loss = loss_fn(output, target)
    
            # Creates gradients
            grad_params = torch.autograd.grad(loss, model.parameters(), create_graph=True)
    
            # Computes the penalty term and adds it to the loss
            grad_norm = 0
            for grad in grad_params:
                grad_norm += grad.pow(2).sum()
            grad_norm = grad_norm.sqrt()
            loss = loss + grad_norm
    
            loss.backward()
    
            # clip gradients here, if desired
    
            optimizer.step()
    

To implement a gradient penalty _with_ gradient scaling, the loss passed to [
` torch.autograd.grad()  ` ](../autograd.html#torch.autograd.grad
"torch.autograd.grad") should be scaled. The resulting gradients will
therefore be scaled, and should be unscaled before being combined to create
the penalty value.

Also, the penalty term computation is part of the forward pass, and therefore
should be inside an [ ` autocast  ` ](../amp.html#torch.cuda.amp.autocast
"torch.cuda.amp.autocast") context.

Here’s how that looks for the same L2 penalty:

    
    
    scaler = GradScaler()
    
    for epoch in epochs:
        for input, target in data:
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            with autocast():
                output = model(input)
                loss = loss_fn(output, target)
    
            # Scales the loss for autograd.grad's backward pass, resulting in scaled grad_params
            scaled_grad_params = torch.autograd.grad(scaler.scale(loss), model.parameters(), create_graph=True)
    
            # Creates unscaled grad_params before computing the penalty. scaled_grad_params are
            # not owned by any optimizer, so ordinary division is used instead of scaler.unscale_:
            inv_scale = 1./scaler.get_scale()
            grad_params = [p * inv_scale for p in scaled_grad_params]
    
            # Computes the penalty term and adds it to the loss
            with autocast():
                grad_norm = 0
                for grad in grad_params:
                    grad_norm += grad.pow(2).sum()
                grad_norm = grad_norm.sqrt()
                loss = loss + grad_norm
    
            # Applies scaling to the backward call as usual.
            # Accumulates leaf gradients that are correctly scaled.
            scaler.scale(loss).backward()
    
            # may unscale_ here if desired (e.g., to allow clipping unscaled gradients)
    
            # step() and update() proceed as usual.
            scaler.step(optimizer)
            scaler.update()

# Real-Time Video Processing with Python and OpenCV: Capturing, Optimizing, and Displaying High Frame Rate Streams

Real-time computer vision applications often demand both speed and accuracy, particularly when processing live video feeds from a webcam. Python, paired with OpenCV, offers a powerful and accessible toolkit for building such applications. In this post, we explore the workflow for capturing video from a locally connected webcam, processing each frame on-the-fly, and displaying the results using `cv2.imshow`. We also discuss performance optimization strategies to sustain high frame rates without sacrificing responsiveness.

---

## Capturing Video from a Webcam

OpenCV’s `VideoCapture` class provides a straightforward interface to access a webcam:

```python
import cv2

cap = cv2.VideoCapture(0)  # 0 selects the default webcam

if not cap.isOpened():
    raise IOError("Cannot open webcam")
```

The parameter passed to `VideoCapture` selects the device index; `0` usually corresponds to the default camera. For systems with multiple webcams, increment the index to choose the desired device.

---

## Processing Frames in Real-Time

Once the webcam feed is open, frames can be read in a loop, processed, and displayed. The `read()` method returns a Boolean success flag and the frame itself as a NumPy array:

```python
while True:
    ret, frame = cap.read()
    if not ret:
        break

    # Example processing: convert to grayscale
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

    cv2.imshow('Live Feed', gray)

    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break
```

Here, `cv2.cvtColor` performs a simple grayscale conversion, but more complex pipelines can be inserted—such as edge detection, object tracking, or neural network inference—depending on the application.

---

## Performance Optimization Strategies

Maintaining high frame rates is critical for smooth user experience and accurate real-time analysis. The following strategies can help optimize performance:

1. **Reduce Frame Size**  
   Smaller frames require fewer processing cycles. Use `cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH, width)` and `cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT, height)` to adjust resolution. For example, 640×480 often suffices for many applications.

2. **Efficient Algorithms**  
   Choose algorithms with lower computational complexity. For preprocessing, prefer operations that can be vectorized over pixel-by-pixel loops.

3. **Skip Frames When Necessary**  
   If processing is too heavy, consider skipping frames to keep latency low, especially for tasks where every single frame is not critical.

4. **Leverage Hardware Acceleration**  
   OpenCV can interface with GPU backends or specialized libraries like OpenCL. Where available, enable these to offload computation from the CPU.

5. **Optimize Data Transfers**  
   Minimize unnecessary copying of frame data. Work directly on arrays returned by `read()` without making redundant deep copies.

---

## Displaying with `cv2.imshow`

`cv2.imshow` is designed for rapid frame display in desktop environments. The method creates a window and renders the given image array. It is essential to call `cv2.waitKey` after each `imshow` to allow the GUI to refresh and handle events. The argument to `waitKey` specifies the delay in milliseconds; for real-time video, `1` or `2` milliseconds is typical.

Example:

```python
cv2.imshow('Processed Video', processed_frame)
if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
    break
```

This loop will update the window quickly enough to provide a seamless video experience.

---

## Cleaning Up Resources

When the processing loop ends, release the webcam and close all OpenCV windows to avoid resource leaks:

```python
cap.release()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()
```

This ensures the camera is freed for other applications and the GUI windows are properly terminated.

---

## Putting It All Together

A minimal, high-performance example might look like this:

```python
import cv2

cap = cv2.VideoCapture(0)
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH, 640)
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT, 480)

while True:
    ret, frame = cap.read()
    if not ret:
        break

    processed = cv2.Canny(frame, 100, 200)  # Edge detection
    cv2.imshow('Edges', processed)

    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

cap.release()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()
```

This script captures live video, applies Canny edge detection to each frame, and displays the results in real-time. By controlling resolution and using efficient algorithms, it can sustain a high frame rate, making it suitable for interactive applications.

---

**Conclusion**  
Python and OpenCV offer a flexible and efficient environment for real-time video capture and processing. By understanding how to read frames, apply transformations, and manage display windows, developers can build responsive computer vision tools. With the right performance adjustments—resolution tuning, algorithm selection, and hardware acceleration—high frame rate streaming becomes achievable even on modest hardware, enabling a wide range of interactive and analytical applications.

# Configuring Travis CI to Run Builds from Multiple Branches

Continuous Integration (CI) pipelines are most effective when they can accommodate a variety of development workflows. In many projects, teams work across multiple branches simultaneously—developing new features, testing experimental changes, or maintaining separate release lines. Travis CI offers flexible configuration options to run builds from multiple branches, allowing developers to tailor their pipeline to these needs. This guide walks through how to set up Travis CI for multi-branch builds, how to manage environment variables across branches, and how to trigger builds manually.

---

## 1. Understanding Multi-Branch Builds in Travis CI

By default, Travis CI will build every branch you push to the remote repository, as long as it contains a `.travis.yml` configuration file. However, you can refine which branches should trigger builds using the `branches` key in the configuration. For example:

```yaml
branches:
  only:
    - master
    - develop
    - feature/*
```

This ensures that builds run for the `master` branch, the `develop` branch, and any branch prefixed with `feature/`. This selective approach helps manage build resources while still supporting parallel development streams.

---

## 2. Setting Environment Variables Per Branch

Different branches often require different environment variables—such as API keys for staging vs. production, or feature flags for testing. Travis CI supports defining environment variables directly in the `.travis.yml` file or via the repository settings in the Travis web interface.

To specify branch-specific variables in `.travis.yml`:

```yaml
env:
  global:
    - COMMON_VAR=value
  matrix:
    - BRANCH_ENV=staging
    - BRANCH_ENV=production
```

You can combine this with conditional logic in your build scripts to apply the correct variables based on the branch name:

```bash
if [ "$TRAVIS_BRANCH" == "develop" ]; then
  export API_URL="https://staging.api.example.com"
elif [ "$TRAVIS_BRANCH" == "master" ]; then
  export API_URL="https://api.example.com"
fi
```

This method provides a clean way to keep sensitive credentials out of source control while still customizing builds per branch.

---

## 3. Leveraging Build Matrices for Branch Testing

A powerful feature in Travis CI is the build matrix, which allows you to run multiple job variations for each branch. This is useful for testing against different language versions, dependency sets, or environment configurations.

Example configuration:

```yaml
language: python
python:
  - "3.8"
  - "3.9"
  - "3.10"
env:
  - DJANGO_VERSION=3.2
  - DJANGO_VERSION=4.0
```

With this setup, Travis CI will run every combination of Python version and Django version for each branch, providing comprehensive coverage across environments.

---

## 4. Triggering Builds Manually

Sometimes you need to run a build without pushing new commits—perhaps to re-test after a dependency update or to validate changes in configuration. Travis CI supports manual build triggering via its web interface.

To trigger a build manually:

1. Navigate to your repository in the Travis CI dashboard.
2. Select the branch you want to build from the branch dropdown.
3. Click the **Trigger Build** button.
4. Optionally, add custom environment variables for that specific run.

This feature is especially useful for branches used in long-term testing or for release candidates that need verification before deployment.

---

## 5. Best Practices

- **Keep branch configurations minimal**: Avoid duplicating large sections of `.travis.yml` for each branch. Use conditional logic and environment variables to handle differences.
- **Secure sensitive data**: Use Travis CI’s encrypted environment variables for credentials and keys, ensuring they are not exposed in logs.
- **Monitor build times**: Multi-branch and matrix builds can increase total build time. Use caching and selective branch builds to optimize.
- **Document branch purposes**: Maintain clear documentation so contributors understand which branches are built automatically and which require manual triggers.

---

By combining selective branch building, targeted environment variables, build matrices, and manual triggers, you can create a Travis CI setup that supports complex workflows without sacrificing efficiency. This approach ensures that every branch receives the appropriate build process, making it easier to manage multiple development streams and ensure quality across the project lifecycle.

# Role Hierarchy System The role hierarchy is crucial for server management and security. It offers a structured way to delegate permissions to users and establish anything from a multi-tiered public server admin system to a trusted buddy in your private server helping out here and there. Here's how the hierarchy works: - Roles follow a top-down structure - Members can only affect users with roles lower than their highest role **Administrator** is the most powerful role permission. It grants all permissions and bypasses all channel restrictions, so be sure to assign this role with extreme caution. 1\. Navigate to **Server Settings > Roles** to find the **Administrator** permission. 2\. In **Edit Role**, select the **Permissions** tab. 3\. Under **Advanced Permissions**, toggle **Administrator** on or off. 4\. Press **Save Changes** to confirm your selection. #### Administrator Permission Toggle in Advanced Permissions Settings ## Manage Roles Users with the **Manage Roles** permission can create and modify roles positioned below their own in the role hierarchy. However, they are limited to assigning only the permissions that they themselves possess, and cannot make any changes to roles that are equal to or positioned above their own role level. For example, if your role lacks the **Ban Members** permission, you cannot grant this permission to other users. **NOTE**: Members cannot ban, kick, or change nicknames of users with equal or higher roles, even if they have those permissions. 1\. Navigate to **Server Settings > Roles** to find the **Manage Roles** permission. 2\. In **Edit Role**, select the **Permissions** tab. 3\. Under **General Server Permissions**, toggle **Manage Roles** on or off. 4\. Press **Save Changes** to confirm your selection. #### Manage Roles Permission Toggle in General Server Permissions Settings When creating new roles, there are a few key points to remember: - The @everyone role acts as the template for all new roles. - New roles are placed at the bottom of the hierarchy (just above @everyone), though administrators can adjust their positions later. - You cannot remove permissions from lower roles that your own role requires to function.

of relations on a subclass of the parent model, you **must** specify the [ `
related_name  `
](../../../ref/models/fields/#django.db.models.ForeignKey.related_name
"django.db.models.ForeignKey.related_name") attribute on each such field. If
you forget, Django will raise a validation error.

For example, using the above ` Place  ` class again, let’s create another
subclass with a [ ` ManyToManyField  `
](../../../ref/models/fields/#django.db.models.ManyToManyField
"django.db.models.ManyToManyField") :

    
    
    class Supplier(Place):
        customers = models.ManyToManyField(Place)
    

This results in the error:

    
    
    Reverse query name for 'Supplier.customers' clashes with reverse query
    name for 'Supplier.place_ptr'.
    
    HINT: Add or change a related_name argument to the definition for
    'Supplier.customers' or 'Supplier.place_ptr'.
    

Adding ` related_name  ` to the ` customers  ` field as follows would resolve
the error: ` models.ManyToManyField(Place,  related_name='provider')  ` .

####  Specifying the parent link field  ¶

As mentioned, Django will automatically create a [ ` OneToOneField  `
](../../../ref/models/fields/#django.db.models.OneToOneField
"django.db.models.OneToOneField") linking your child class back to any non-
abstract parent models. If you want to control the name of the attribute
linking back to the parent, you can create your own [ ` OneToOneField  `
](../../../ref/models/fields/#django.db.models.OneToOneField
"django.db.models.OneToOneField") and set [ ` parent_link=True  `
](../../../ref/models/fields/#django.db.models.OneToOneField.parent_link
"django.db.models.OneToOneField.parent_link") to indicate that your field is
the link back to the parent class.

###  Proxy models  ¶

When using  multi-table inheritance  , a new database table is created for
each subclass of a model. This is usually the desired behavior, since the
subclass needs a place to store any additional data fields that are not
present on the base class. Sometimes, however, you only want to change the
Python behavior of a model – perhaps to change the default manager, or add a
new method.

This is what proxy model inheritance is for: creating a _proxy_ for the
original model. You can create, delete and update instances of the proxy model
and all the data will be saved as if you were using the original (non-proxied)
model. The difference is that you can change things like the default model
ordering or the default manager in the proxy, without having to alter the
original.

Proxy models are declared like normal models. You tell Django that it’s a
proxy model by setting the [ ` proxy  `
](../../../ref/models/options/#django.db.models.Options.proxy
"django.db.models.Options.proxy") attribute of the ` Meta  ` class to ` True
` .
