           **--proxy-type** _proto_ (Specify proxy protocol)
               In connect mode, this option requests the protocol _proto_ to
               connect through the proxy host specified by **--proxy**. In
               listen mode, this option has Ncat act as a proxy server using
               the specified protocol.
    
               The currently available protocols in connect mode are http
               (CONNECT), socks4 (SOCKSv4), and socks5 (SOCKSv5). The only
               server currently supported is http. If this option is not
               used, the default protocol is http.
    
           **--proxy-auth** _user_**[:**_pass_] (Specify proxy credentials)
               In connect mode, gives the credentials that will be used to
               connect to the proxy server. In listen mode, gives the
               credentials that will be required of connecting clients. For
               use with **--proxy-type http** or **--proxy-type socks5** , the form
               should be username:password. For **--proxy-type socks4** , it
               should be a username only.
    
               These credentials can be alternatively passed onto Ncat by
               setting environment variable **NCAT_PROXY_AUTH** , which reduces
               the risk of the credentials being captured in process logs.
               (Option **--proxy-auth** takes precedence.)
    
           **--proxy-dns** _type_ (Specify where to resolve proxy destination)
               In connect mode, it provides control over whether proxy
               destination hostnames are resolved by the remote proxy server
               or locally, by Ncat itself. Possible values for _type_ are:
    
               local - Hostnames are resolved locally on the Ncat host. Ncat
               exits with error if the hostname cannot be resolved.
    
               remote - Hostnames are passed directly onto the remote proxy
               server. This is the default behavior.
    
               both - Hostname resolution is first attempted on the Ncat
               host. Unresolvable hostnames are passed onto the remote proxy
               server.
    
               none - Hostname resolution is completely disabled. Only a
               literal IPv4 or IPv6 address can be used as the proxy
               destination.
    
               Local hostname resolution generally respects IP version
               specified with options **-4** or **-6** , except for SOCKS4, which is
               incompatible with IPv6.

##  Parquet  #

[ Apache Parquet ](https://parquet.apache.org/) provides a partitioned binary
columnar serialization for data frames. It is designed to make reading and
writing data frames efficient, and to make sharing data across data analysis
languages easy. Parquet can use a variety of compression techniques to shrink
the file size as much as possible while still maintaining good read
performance.

Parquet is designed to faithfully serialize and de-serialize ` DataFrame  ` s,
supporting all of the pandas dtypes, including extension dtypes such as
datetime with tz.

Several caveats.

  * Duplicate column names and non-string columns names are not supported. 

  * The ` pyarrow  ` engine always writes the index to the output, but ` fastparquet  ` only writes non-default indexes. This extra column can cause problems for non-pandas consumers that are not expecting it. You can force including or omitting indexes with the ` index  ` argument, regardless of the underlying engine. 

  * Index level names, if specified, must be strings. 

  * In the ` pyarrow  ` engine, categorical dtypes for non-string types can be serialized to parquet, but will de-serialize as their primitive dtype. 

  * The ` pyarrow  ` engine preserves the ` ordered  ` flag of categorical dtypes with string types. ` fastparquet  ` does not preserve the ` ordered  ` flag. 

  * Non supported types include ` Interval  ` and actual Python object types. These will raise a helpful error message on an attempt at serialization. ` Period  ` type is supported with pyarrow >= 0.16.0. 

  * The ` pyarrow  ` engine preserves extension data types such as the nullable integer and string data type (requiring pyarrow >= 0.16.0, and requiring the extension type to implement the needed protocols, see the [ extension types documentation  ](../development/extending.html#extending-extension-arrow) ). 

You can specify an ` engine  ` to direct the serialization. This can be one of
` pyarrow  ` , or ` fastparquet  ` , or ` auto  ` . If the engine is NOT
specified, then the ` pd.options.io.parquet.engine  ` option is checked; if
this is also ` auto  ` , then ` pyarrow  ` is tried, and falling back to `
fastparquet  ` .

See the documentation for [ pyarrow ](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/)
and [ fastparquet ](https://fastparquet.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) .

Note

These engines are very similar and should read/write nearly identical parquet
format files. ` pyarrow>=8.0.0  ` supports timedelta data, `
fastparquet>=0.1.4  ` supports timezone aware datetimes. These libraries
differ by having different underlying dependencies ( ` fastparquet  ` by using
` numba  ` , while ` pyarrow  ` uses a c-library).

# Designing Ergonomic Hotkey Layouts for Maximum Productivity  

For many productivity-focused applications, the keyboard is the fastest route to executing commands. Well-designed hotkey layouts can significantly reduce the time spent navigating menus, clicking buttons, or moving between tools. Yet, not all hotkey systems are created equal—poor layouts can lead to strain, confusion, and slower workflows. By applying ergonomic principles and memory-friendly design strategies, developers and power users can build hotkey schemes that feel natural, minimize physical effort, and enhance overall efficiency.  

## Ergonomic Placement: The Foundation of Comfort  

The physical arrangement of keys on a keyboard directly impacts user comfort. Ergonomic placement begins with understanding the "home row" and the natural resting position of the hands. Keys that require frequent use should be positioned within easy reach of the index and middle fingers, avoiding excessive stretching or twisting of the wrist.  

For example, assigning common commands to keys near **ASDF** and **JKL;** allows users to execute them with minimal movement. Hotkeys that require modifier keys—such as `Ctrl`, `Alt`, or `Shift`—should be paired with letters or numbers that can be pressed without moving the hand far from its resting position. This reduces strain during long sessions and keeps hand movements fluid.  

## Grouping and Logical Clustering  

Beyond physical reach, hotkey layouts benefit greatly from logical clustering. Commands that are conceptually related should be grouped together on the keyboard. For instance, if an application has navigation commands like "Next Tab" and "Previous Tab," placing them on adjacent keys (e.g., `Ctrl+Tab` and `Ctrl+Shift+Tab`) helps reinforce their relationship in the user’s mind.  

Clustering also aids in quick recall. If editing commands—like cut, copy, and paste—are grouped in a similar modifier pattern (`Ctrl+X`, `Ctrl+C`, `Ctrl+V`), users can rely on muscle memory rather than consciously searching for the correct key sequence. This design principle is especially useful in complex applications where dozens of hotkeys exist.  

## Minimizing Overlap and Conflict  

A common pitfall in hotkey design is overlapping assignments that cause conflicts or unintended actions. This often happens when default system-wide shortcuts are overridden by application-specific ones, leading to confusion. To avoid this, developers should audit the operating system’s common hotkeys and either avoid duplication or ensure that the application’s override is intentional and well-documented.  

Similarly, within the application itself, each hotkey should have a unique and clearly defined function. Redundancy can be helpful in rare cases—such as offering alternative shortcuts for accessibility—but should be implemented with care to prevent accidental triggers.  

## Progressive Memorization Techniques  

Even the most ergonomic layout is useless if users cannot remember it. Progressive memorization strategies can bridge this gap. One effective approach is **incremental introduction**—introducing hotkeys gradually rather than overwhelming users with a full set at once.  

Applications can highlight relevant shortcuts in tooltips, menus, or on-screen prompts during use. Over time, repeated exposure builds familiarity, leading to unconscious execution. Another method is to allow users to customize their own hotkeys; self-assigned shortcuts tend to be easier to recall because they are based on personal logic and preference.  

## Visual Reinforcement and Training  

Visual reinforcement can speed up the memorization process. Cheat sheets, overlay guides, and quick-reference panels offer immediate lookup without disrupting workflow. Some applications integrate interactive training modes where users practice common hotkey sequences in a controlled environment, improving muscle memory and confidence.  

Color coding in on-screen guides can also help—for example, using one color for navigation commands, another for editing, and a third for formatting. This visual grouping mirrors the logical clustering principle and strengthens cognitive association.  

## Balancing Speed and Accessibility  

While speed is the primary goal for most hotkey layouts, accessibility should not be overlooked. Users with limited mobility or repetitive strain injuries may require alternative configurations. Options such as single-key shortcuts, voice command integration, or programmable input devices can make the application more inclusive.  

Designers should also consider the diversity of keyboard hardware—laptop keyboards, mechanical boards, and ergonomic split designs all have different layouts and spacing. Testing hotkey schemes across multiple devices ensures that the chosen configuration remains comfortable and efficient for a wide audience.  

## Conclusion  

Hotkeys are more than just a convenience—they are a powerful tool for shaping user workflow. By focusing on ergonomic placement, logical grouping, conflict avoidance, and memorization support, developers can create hotkey systems that feel intuitive and reduce physical strain. Thoughtful design not only speeds up interaction but also makes long-term use more sustainable and enjoyable. In productivity applications where every second counts, a well-optimized keyboard layout can be the difference between a smooth, efficient experience and a frustrating one.

# Optimizing Django ORM Queries for High-Performance Applications

When working with Django’s ORM in production-scale environments, the efficiency of database access can make or break application performance. As datasets grow and relational complexity increases, the number of queries executed per request can escalate quickly—leading to latency, unnecessary load, and scalability concerns. This article explores advanced strategies for reducing query counts and improving throughput, focusing on `select_related`, `prefetch_related`, and practical profiling techniques.

---

## Understanding Query Overhead

By default, Django’s ORM lazily loads related objects. While this approach is convenient, it can lead to the *N+1 query problem*—where fetching a set of objects and their related data results in one query for the initial set and an additional query for each related object. In large datasets, this pattern can cause significant performance degradation.

For example:

```python
orders = Order.objects.all()
for order in orders:
    print(order.customer.name)
```

In this scenario, each `order.customer` access triggers a separate query unless explicitly optimized. The solution is to instruct Django to perform joins or prefetches in a single query set.

---

## Leveraging `select_related`

`select_related` is best suited for foreign key and one-to-one relationships. It performs a SQL join, retrieving related object fields in the same query:

```python
orders = Order.objects.select_related('customer').all()
```

This approach reduces the number of queries to one, regardless of the number of orders processed. It is particularly effective when the related model data is always needed in the view or template.

---

## Using `prefetch_related`

For many-to-many and reverse foreign key relationships, `prefetch_related` is the preferred option. It performs multiple queries but caches the results, avoiding repeated lookups:

```python
orders = Order.objects.prefetch_related('items').all()
```

Here, Django fetches all orders in one query and then retrieves all related `items` in a second query, storing them in memory for subsequent access. This prevents the ORM from issuing a query per order when iterating over `order.items.all()`.

---

## Combining Strategies

In complex applications, combining `select_related` and `prefetch_related` can yield optimal results:

```python
orders = (
    Order.objects
    .select_related('customer', 'address')
    .prefetch_related('items', 'payments')
)
```

This hybrid approach minimizes query counts for both direct and reverse relationships, ensuring data is ready for immediate use in templates or business logic.

---

## Profiling with Django Debug Toolbar

Before applying optimizations, it is crucial to identify bottlenecks. The [Django Debug Toolbar](https://django-debug-toolbar.readthedocs.io/) provides a real-time breakdown of queries executed during a request, including SQL statements, execution time, and call stacks.

To use it effectively:

1. Install and configure in your `INSTALLED_APPS`.
2. Load a page in development mode.
3. Review the SQL panel to see query counts and duplication.
4. Adjust QuerySets using `select_related` or `prefetch_related` where excessive queries are detected.

This iterative approach ensures changes are data-driven rather than speculative.

---

## Adjusting QuerySet Usage for Scalability

Beyond relationship loading, consider the following best practices:

- **Limit Fields**: Use `.only()` or `.defer()` to restrict columns fetched when full model data is unnecessary.
- **Batch Processing**: Apply `.iterator()` for memory efficiency when processing large datasets.
- **Filter Early**: Apply `.filter()` and `.exclude()` before expensive joins to reduce result sets.
- **Avoid Overfetching**: Resist the temptation to prefetch data that is not consistently required.

---

## Conclusion

Efficient database access in Django hinges on understanding how the ORM retrieves related data and proactively managing query execution. By combining `select_related` and `prefetch_related`, leveraging profiling tools like Django Debug Toolbar, and refining QuerySet usage, developers can achieve significant performance improvements. In high-traffic applications, these optimizations translate directly into faster response times, reduced server load, and improved scalability—all critical factors in delivering a robust user experience.

# Visualizing Weighted Averages in Historical Financial Data with Tableau  

When working with financial datasets that span multiple time periods, weighted averages are often a more accurate representation of trends than simple averages. This is especially true when dealing with price data influenced by varying transaction volumes, quantities, or market weights. Tableau, with its rich visualization capabilities, offers a powerful platform for turning complex weighted calculations into clear, interactive dashboards that aid in decision-making.  

## Understanding the Role of Weighted Averages in Financial Analysis  

In historical financial datasets—such as stock prices, commodity rates, or retail transaction data—each data point may carry a different level of significance. For example, a price derived from a high-volume trading day should have more influence on a trend line than one from a low-volume day. Weighted averages account for these differences by incorporating a measure of importance (often quantity or volume) into the calculation, producing a more representative metric over time.  

When visualized properly, weighted averages help stakeholders quickly identify patterns that could be obscured by unweighted calculations. The challenge lies in ensuring the visualization is both accurate and intuitive, particularly for audiences who may not be familiar with the underlying math.  

## Best Practices for Designing Weighted Average Dashboards in Tableau  

### 1. **Create a Clean and Consistent Date Axis**  
Financial data often comes with irregular intervals or missing dates. Before building charts, ensure your date field is standardized and continuous where appropriate. Tableau’s date hierarchy tools can help you drill down from years to months to specific days, allowing users to explore weighted averages across different time frames without losing context.  

### 2. **Integrate Weighting Directly into Calculated Fields**  
The core of weighted average visualization is the calculation itself. In Tableau, this typically involves creating calculated fields that multiply each value by its corresponding weight, sum those products, and divide by the total weight for the chosen period. Embedding this calculation in Tableau ensures that filters and parameters dynamically update the weighted average when the user changes the view.  

### 3. **Choose Appropriate Chart Types**  
For time-series weighted averages, line charts are often the most effective. They clearly show trends over time and can be enhanced with markers to indicate significant events or thresholds. Consider using dual-axis charts to compare weighted averages against raw averages, helping viewers understand the impact of weighting.  

### 4. **Use Color and Highlighting Strategically**  
Weighted averages can be paired with conditional formatting to flag unusual movements. For example, a sudden drop in a weighted average price might be highlighted in red, while steady upward trends could be shown in green. This visual cueing draws attention to key points without requiring users to interpret raw numbers.  

### 5. **Enable Interactive Filtering and Drill-Down**  
A well-designed Tableau dashboard should allow users to filter by categories, regions, or product types to see how weighted averages vary across different segments. Parameters can let viewers adjust the weighting factor—switching from quantity-based weighting to revenue-based weighting, for example—providing deeper insight into the dataset.  

### 6. **Annotate for Context**  
Numbers alone rarely tell the full story. Use Tableau’s annotation tools to explain spikes or dips in the weighted average line. Linking annotations to external data sources, such as market news or company reports, helps contextualize trends and adds narrative depth to the visualization.  

## Enhancing Presentation Impact  

When presenting weighted average visualizations, clarity and accessibility are key. Avoid overloading the dashboard with too many metrics; instead, focus on the weighted average as the central measure, supported by supplementary charts or tables. Tooltips can be configured to show the underlying data points and weights, giving interested viewers a way to validate the calculation without cluttering the main view.  

Finally, consider exporting snapshots of critical time periods as static images for inclusion in reports, while keeping the interactive dashboard available for deeper exploration. This hybrid approach ensures that both high-level summaries and granular analyses are accessible to different audience types.  

## Conclusion  

Weighted averages provide a nuanced view of historical financial data, helping analysts and decision-makers capture the true significance of each data point. Tableau’s flexibility in calculated fields, interactivity, and design customization makes it an ideal tool for presenting these metrics effectively. By focusing on clean date handling, thoughtful chart design, and interactive features, you can create dashboards that not only calculate weighted averages accurately but also make them visually compelling and easy to interpret—turning complex data into actionable insights.

# Modularizing Python Code with Object-Oriented Principles

When working on large Python projects, code organization becomes a critical factor in maintainability, scalability, and collaborative development. One of the most effective strategies for managing complexity is to split source code into modular components, particularly by separating classes and functions into distinct files or packages. This approach allows developers to isolate responsibilities, reuse components, and keep imports consistent across the project.

## The Rationale for Modularization

As a project grows, the temptation to keep adding functions and classes into a single script can lead to a monolithic structure that is difficult to navigate. Modularization addresses this challenge by breaking down the code into smaller, logically grouped units.  
For example, in an application with data models, business logic, and user interface components, each layer can reside in a separate module. This separation makes it easier to understand the purpose of each file, identify dependencies, and apply changes without unintended side effects elsewhere in the codebase.

Object-oriented programming (OOP) naturally lends itself to modularization. Classes encapsulate data and behavior, so moving them into dedicated modules aligns with the principle of single responsibility. A `User` class might reside in `models/user.py`, while a `UserService` class could be placed in `services/user_service.py`. This structure mirrors the logical architecture of the application.

## Structuring Modules for Classes and Functions

A common pattern involves creating a package directory with an `__init__.py` file, and then placing related modules inside it. For instance:

```
project/
    models/
        __init__.py
        user.py
        product.py
    services/
        __init__.py
        user_service.py
        product_service.py
    utils/
        __init__.py
        date_utils.py
        string_utils.py
```

Within `user.py`, the `User` class can be defined independently of other models:

```python
class User:
    def __init__(self, username, email):
        self.username = username
        self.email = email
```

In `user_service.py`, the logic that operates on `User` instances is encapsulated:

```python
from models.user import User

class UserService:
    def create_user(self, username, email):
        return User(username, email)
```

This separation ensures that data structures and business logic remain distinct, while imports clearly reflect dependencies.

## Maintaining Consistent Imports

Splitting code into multiple modules introduces the need for careful import management. Inconsistent or circular imports can cause runtime errors or make the code harder to follow.

To maintain consistency:

1. **Use absolute imports** within the project to clarify the module path:
   ```python
   from project.models.user import User
   ```
   
2. **Avoid circular dependencies** by restructuring modules so that higher-level components depend on lower-level ones, but not vice versa.

3. **Centralize common imports** in a single module if they are used frequently across the codebase. For example, `utils/__init__.py` can expose functions from multiple utility modules.

4. **Document the import structure** in developer guidelines to ensure that all contributors follow the same conventions.

## Benefits Beyond Readability

Modularizing code not only improves readability but also facilitates testing. Unit tests can target individual modules without having to load the entire application. This isolation speeds up test execution and makes it easier to pinpoint failures.

Moreover, modularization supports reusability. A well-designed module can be imported into different projects without modification. For instance, a `date_utils.py` module containing functions for parsing and formatting dates can be shared across applications.

In collaborative environments, modular design enables parallel development. Different team members can work on separate modules without interfering with each other’s changes, reducing merge conflicts and improving productivity.

## Conclusion

Splitting Python source files into modular components using object-oriented principles is a foundational practice for building robust, maintainable applications. By placing classes and functions into logically organized modules, developers can achieve clearer separation of concerns, consistent imports, and improved testability. Establishing a thoughtful module structure early in the project lifecycle pays dividends in scalability and team efficiency, ensuring that the codebase remains manageable as it evolves.

#  pmdatrivial(1) — Linux manual page

NAME  |  SYNOPSIS  |  DESCRIPTION  |  INSTALLATION  |  FILES  |  PCP ENVIRONMENT  |  SEE ALSO  |  COLOPHON   
---  
|  
      
    
    _PMDATRIVIAL_(1)           General Commands Manual          _PMDATRIVIAL_(1)
    

##  NAME  top

    
    
           **pmdatrivial** - trivial performance metrics domain agent (PMDA)
    

##  SYNOPSIS  top

    
    
           **$PCP_PMDAS_DIR/trivial/pmdatrivial**[**-d** _domain_] [**-l** _logfile_] [**-U**
           _username_]
    

##  DESCRIPTION  top

    
    
           **pmdatrivial** is the simplest possible Performance Metrics Domain
           Agent (PMDA) which exports a single performance metric, the time
           in seconds since the 1st of January, 1970.
    
           The trivial PMDA is shipped as source code and is designed to be
           an aid for PMDA developers.
    
           A brief description of the **pmdatrivial** command line options
           follows:
    
           **-d** It is absolutely crucial that the performance metrics _domain_
                number specified here is unique and consistent.  That is,
                _domain_ should be different for every PMDA on the one host,
                and the same _domain_ number should be used for the same PMDA
                on all hosts.
    
           **-l** Location of the log file.  By default, a log file named
                _trivial.log_ is written in the current directory of [pmcd(1)](../man1/pmcd.1.html)
                when **pmdatrivial** is started, i.e.  **$PCP_LOG_DIR/pmcd**.  If
                the log file cannot be created or is not writable, output is
                written to the standard error instead.
    
           **-U** User account under which to run the agent.  The default is
                the unprivileged "pcp" account in current versions of PCP,
                but in older versions the superuser account ("root") was
                used by default.
    

##  INSTALLATION  top

    
    
           If you want access to the names, help text and values for the
           trivial performance metrics, do the following as root:
    
                # cd $PCP_PMDAS_DIR/trivial
                # ./Install
    
           If you want to undo the installation, do the following as root:
    
                # cd $PCP_PMDAS_DIR/trivial
                # ./Remove
    
           **pmdatrivial** is launched by [pmcd(1)](../man1/pmcd.1.html) and should never be executed
           directly.  The Install and Remove scripts notify [pmcd(1)](../man1/pmcd.1.html) when the
           agent is installed or removed.
    

##  FILES  top

    
    
           **$PCP_PMCDCONF_PATH**
                  command line options used to launch **pmdatrivial**
           **$PCP_PMDAS_DIR/trivial/help**
                  default help text file for the trivial metrics
           **$PCP_PMDAS_DIR/trivial/Install**
                  installation script for the **pmdatrivial** agent
           **$PCP_PMDAS_DIR/trivial/Remove**
                  undo installation script for the **pmdatrivial** agent
           **$PCP_LOG_DIR/pmcd/trivial.log**
                  default log file for error messages and other information
                  from **pmdatrivial**
    

##  PCP ENVIRONMENT  top

    
    
           Environment variables with the prefix **PCP_** are used to
           parameterize the file and directory names used by PCP.  On each
           installation, the file **/etc/pcp.conf** contains the local values
           for these variables.  The **$PCP_CONF** variable may be used to
           specify an alternative configuration file, as described in
           [pcp.conf(5)](../man5/pcp.conf.5.html).
    

##  SEE ALSO  top

    
    
           [PCPIntro(1)](../man1/PCPIntro.1.html), [pmcd(1)]

###  Limits on filling while reindexing  #

The ` limit  ` and ` tolerance  ` arguments provide additional control over
filling while reindexing. Limit specifies the maximum count of consecutive
matches:

    
    
    In [237]: ts2.reindex(ts.index, method="ffill", limit=1)
    Out[237]: 
    2000-01-03    0.183051
    2000-01-04    0.183051
    2000-01-05         NaN
    2000-01-06    2.395489
    2000-01-07    2.395489
    2000-01-08         NaN
    2000-01-09    0.733639
    2000-01-10    0.733639
    Freq: D, dtype: float64
    

In contrast, tolerance specifies the maximum distance between the index and
indexer values:

    
    
    In [238]: ts2.reindex(ts.index, method="ffill", tolerance="1 day")
    Out[238]: 
    2000-01-03    0.183051
    2000-01-04    0.183051
    2000-01-05         NaN
    2000-01-06    2.395489
    2000-01-07    2.395489
    2000-01-08         NaN
    2000-01-09    0.733639
    2000-01-10    0.733639
    Freq: D, dtype: float64
    

Notice that when used on a ` DatetimeIndex  ` , ` TimedeltaIndex  ` or `
PeriodIndex  ` , ` tolerance  ` will coerced into a ` Timedelta  ` if
possible. This allows you to specify tolerance with appropriate strings.

**[Forum Thread]**  
**Topic:** Changing Linux Server Hostname with `hostnamectl` – Best Practices & Examples  

---

**Original Post by sysadmin_joe:**  
Hey folks,  
I’ve been setting up a few new VMs for our internal dev environment, and I need to make sure their hostnames are configured properly before they go live. I know you can use `hostnamectl` to change the hostname, but I’m wondering if there are any gotchas I should watch for—especially around formatting the name and avoiding conflicts on our network.  

Any tips or examples of how you format yours would be great. Also, is there a preferred way to ensure the change sticks after reboot?  

---

**Reply by linux_guru:**  
Sure thing, Joe. The `hostnamectl` utility is part of `systemd` and is pretty straightforward. The basic syntax to set a static hostname is:  

```bash
sudo hostnamectl set-hostname new-hostname
```  

This will update the static hostname stored in `/etc/hostname` and also apply the transient hostname in the current session. It persists across reboots.  

**Formatting tips:**  
- Stick to lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens (`-`).  
- Avoid underscores; they’re technically allowed in some contexts, but certain services and DNS setups can misinterpret them.  
- Hostnames should start and end with alphanumeric characters (no hyphen at the start or end).  
- Keep it under 63 characters—this is a DNS limit and a safe practice.  

Example:  
```bash
sudo hostnamectl set-hostname dev-app-01
```  

---

**Reply by netops_maria:**  
One important thing is to check for conflicts before setting the hostname. In larger networks, duplicate hostnames can cause confusion in monitoring tools, SSH host key mismatches, and even service discovery errors.  

I recommend doing a quick `ping` or checking your DNS records to ensure the name isn’t already in use:  

```bash
ping dev-app-01
```  

If you get a reply from an unexpected IP, pick another name.  

---

**Reply by cloud_admin:**  
Adding to Maria’s point—if your network uses DHCP with dynamic DNS updates, changing a hostname may trigger an update in your DNS zone. Make sure your DHCP server is configured to accept and process those updates, or you might end up with stale records.  

Also, after changing the hostname, it’s a good idea to update `/etc/hosts` so local services resolve it correctly:  

```bash
127.0.0.1   localhost
127.0.1.1   dev-app-01
```  

---

**Reply by devops_tom:**  
For environments with multiple tiers (dev, staging, prod), we use a naming convention that encodes the environment and role:  

`<env>-<service>-<number>`  

Examples:  
- `dev-api-01`  
- `stg-db-02`  
- `prod-web-03`  

This makes it easy to identify the server’s purpose just from the hostname and reduces the chance of collisions.  

---

**Reply by unix_veteran:**  
One more tip—`hostnamectl` also lets you set the “pretty” hostname, which is more human-friendly and can include spaces. It won’t affect DNS or machine identification but shows up in GUIs and some logs:  

```bash
sudo hostnamectl set-hostname "Development App Server" --pretty
```  

You can check your current settings with:  

```bash
hostnamectl status
```  

This will display the static, transient, and pretty hostnames.  

---

**Reply by sysadmin_joe:**  
Thanks all! I ended up using:  

```bash
sudo hostnamectl set-hostname dev-api-01
```  

and updated `/etc/hosts` accordingly. The change persisted after reboot and didn’t conflict with anything in our DNS. I’ll stick to the naming convention Tom suggested for future servers.  

---

**Moderator Note:**  
For anyone reading this later:  
- Always verify hostname uniqueness on your network before changing it.  
- Follow RFC 1123 guidelines for valid hostname characters.  
- Remember to update `/etc/hosts` and, if applicable, inform your DNS or DHCP infrastructure of the change.  

---

A client can ask that credentials should be included in cross-site requests in
one of two ways:

  * Using [ ` fetch() ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/API/fetch) , by setting the [ ` credentials ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/API/Request/Request#credentials) option in the [ ` Request() ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/API/Request/Request "Request\(\)") constructor to ` "include" ` . 
  * Using [ ` XMLHttpRequest ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest) , by setting the [ ` XMLHttpRequest.withCredentials ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest/withCredentials) property to ` true ` . 

If the client has asked for credentials to be included:

  * If the request is [ preflighted ](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Preflight_request) , then the preflight request does not include credentials. If the server's response to the preflight request sets the ` Access-Control-Allow-Credentials ` header to ` true ` , then the real request will include credentials: otherwise, the browser reports a network error. 
  * If the request is not preflighted, then the request will include credentials, and if the server's response does not set the ` Access-Control-Allow-Credentials ` header to ` true ` , the browser reports a network error. 

Header type  |  [ Response header ](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Response_header)  
---|---  
[ Forbidden header name ](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Forbidden_header_name) |  no   
  
##  Syntax

http

    
    
    Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
    

##  Directives

` true `

    

The only valid value for this header is ` true ` (case-sensitive). If you
don't need credentials, omit this header entirely (rather than setting its
value to ` false ` ).

##  Examples

Allow credentials:

http

    
    
    Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
    

Using [ ` fetch() ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/API/fetch) with credentials:

js

    
    
    fetch(url, {
      credentials: "include",
    });
    

Using [ ` XMLHttpRequest ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest) with
credentials:

js

    
    
    const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
    xhr.open("GET", "http://example.com/", true);
    xhr.withCredentials = true;
    xhr.send(null);

## Template inheritance ¶ The most powerful – and thus the most complex – part of Django’s template engine is template inheritance. Template inheritance allows you to build a base “skeleton” template that contains all the common elements of your site and defines **blocks** that child templates can override. Let’s look at template inheritance by starting with an example: {% block title %}My amazing site{% endblock %}
{% block sidebar %}
  • Home
  • Blog
{% endblock %}
{% block content %}{% endblock %}
This template, which we’ll call ` base.html ` , defines an HTML skeleton document that you might use for a two-column page. It’s the job of “child” templates to fill the empty blocks with content. In this example, the [ ` block ` ](../builtins/#std-templatetag-block) tag defines three blocks that child templates can fill in. All the [ ` block ` ](../builtins/#std-templatetag-block) tag does is to tell the template engine that a child template may override those portions of the template. A child template might look like this: {% extends "base.html" %} {% block title %}My amazing blog{% endblock %} {% block content %} {% for entry in blog_entries %}

{{ entry.title }}

{{ entry.body }}

{% endfor %} {% endblock %} The [ ` extends ` ](../builtins/#std-templatetag-extends) tag is the key here. It tells the template engine that this template “extends” another template. When the template system evaluates this template, first it locates the parent – in this case, “base.html”. At that point, the template engine will notice the three [ ` block ` ](../builtins/#std-templatetag-block) tags in ` base.html ` and replace those blocks with the contents of the child template. Depending on the value of ` blog_entries ` , the output might look like: My amazing blog
  • Home
  • Blog

Entry one

This is my first entry.

Entry two

This is my second entry.

Note that since the child template didn’t define the ` sidebar ` block, the value from the parent template is used instead. Content within a ` {% block %} ` tag in a parent template is always used as a fallback. You can use as many levels of inheritance as needed. One common way of using inheritance is the following three-level approach: * Create a ` base.html ` template that holds the main look-and-feel of your site. * Create a ` base_SECTIONNAME.html ` template for each “section” of your site. For example, ` base_news.html ` , ` base_sports.html ` . These templates all extend ` base.html ` and include section-specific styles/design. * Create individual templates for each type of page, such as a news article or blog entry. These templates extend the appropriate section template. This approach maximizes code reuse and helps to add items to shared content areas, such as section-wide navigation. merge two or more arrays. This method does not change the existing arrays, but
instead returns a new array.

##  Try it

##  Syntax

js

    
    
    concat()
    concat(value1)
    concat(value1, value2)
    concat(value1, value2, /* â¦, */ valueN)
    

###  Parameters

` value1 ` , â¦, ` valueN ` Optional

    

Arrays and/or values to concatenate into a new array. If all ` valueN `
parameters are omitted, ` concat ` returns a [ shallow copy ](/en-
US/docs/Glossary/Shallow_copy) of the existing array on which it is called.
See the description below for more details.

###  Return value

A new [ ` Array ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array)
instance.

##  Description

The ` concat ` method creates a new array. The array will first be populated
by the elements in the object on which it is called. Then, for each argument,
its value will be concatenated into the array â for normal objects or
primitives, the argument itself will become an element of the final array; for
arrays or array-like objects with the property [ ` Symbol.isConcatSpreadable `
](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Symbol/isConcatSpreadable) set
to a truthy value, each element of the argument will be independently added to
the final array. The ` concat ` method does not recurse into nested array
arguments.

The ` concat() ` method is a [ copying method ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array#copying_methods_and_mutating_methods)
. It does not alter ` this ` or any of the arrays provided as arguments but
instead returns a [ shallow copy ](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Shallow_copy) that
contains the same elements as the ones from the original arrays.

The ` concat() ` method preserves empty slots if any of the source arrays is [
sparse ](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Indexed_collections#sparse_arrays) .

The ` concat() ` method is [ generic ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array#generic_array_methods) .
The ` this ` value is treated in the same way as the other arguments (except
it will be converted to an object first), which means plain objects will be
directly prepended to the resulting array, while array-like objects with
truthy ` @@isConcatSpreadable ` will be spread into the resulting array.

##  Examples

###  Concatenating two arrays

The following code concatenates two arrays:

js

    
    
    const letters = ["a", "b", "c"];
    const numbers = [1, 2, 3];
    
    const alphaNumeric = letters.concat(numbers);
    console.log(alphaNumeric);
    // results in ['a', 'b', 'c', 1, 2, 3]
    

###  Concatenating three arrays

The following code concatenates three arrays:

js

    
    
    const num1 = [1, 2, 3];
    const num2 = [4, 5, 6];
    const num3 = [7, 8, 9];
    
    const numbers = num1.concat(num2, num3);
    
    console.log(numbers);
    // results in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]
    

###  Concatenating values to an array

The following code concatenates three values to an array:

js

    
    
    const letters = ["a", "b", "c"];
    
    const alphaNumeric = letters.concat(1, [2, 3]);
    
    console.log(alphaNumeric);
    // results in ['a', 'b', 'c', 1, 2, 3]
    

###  Concatenating nested arrays

The following code concatenates nested arrays and demonstrates retention of
references:

js

    
    
    const num1 = [[1]];
    const num2 = [2, [3]];
    
    const numbers = num1.concat(num2);
    
    console.log(numbers);
    // results in [[1], 2, [3]]
    
    // modify the first element of num1
    num1[0].push(4);
    
    console.log(numbers);
    // results in [[1, 4], 2, [3]]
    

###  Concatenating array-like objects with Symbol.isConcatSpreadable

` concat ` does not treat all array-like objects as arrays by default â only
if ` Symbol.isConcatSpreadable ` is set to a truthy value (e.g. ` true ` ).

the starting position of the first match or \\(-1\\) if there is none, with
attribute ` "match.length" ` , an integer vector giving the length of the
matched text (or \\(-1\\) for no match). The match positions and lengths are

which is of the same form as the return value for ` regexpr ` , except that

` regexec ` returns a list of the same length as ` text ` each element of
which is either \\(-1\\) if there is no match, or a sequence of integers with
the starting positions of the match and all substrings corresponding to
parenthesized subexpressions of ` pattern ` , with attribute ` "match.length"

Where matching failed because of resource limits (especially for PCRE) this is
regarded as a non-match, usually with a warning.

##  Warning

The POSIX 1003.2 mode of ` gsub ` and ` gregexpr ` does not work correctly
with repeated word-boundaries (e.g., ` pattern = "\b" ` ). Use ` perl = TRUE `
for such matches (but that may not work as expected with non-ASCII inputs, as
the meaning of ‘word’ is system-dependent).

##  Performance considerations

If you are doing a lot of regular expression matching, including on very long
strings, you will want to consider the options used. Generally PCRE will be
faster than the default regular expression engine, and ` fixed = TRUE ` faster
still (especially when each pattern is matched only a few times).

If you are working in a single-byte locale and have marked UTF-8 strings that
are representable in that locale, convert them first as just one UTF-8 string
will force all the matching to be done in Unicode, which attracts a penalty of
around \\(3\times{}\\) for the default POSIX 1003.2 mode.

If you can make use of ` useBytes = TRUE ` , the strings will not be checked
before matching, and the actual matching will be faster. Often byte-based
matching suffices in a UTF-8 locale since byte patterns of one character never
match part of another.

PCRE-based matching by default puts additional effort into ‘studying’ the
compiled pattern when ` x ` / ` text ` has length at least 10. As from  R
3.4.0 that study may use the PCRE JIT compiler on platforms where it is
available (see ` [ pcre_config ](/link/pcre_config?package=base&version=3.6.2)
` ). The details are controlled by ` [ options
](/link/options?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` ` PCRE_study ` and `
PCRE_use_JIT ` . (Some timing comparisons can be seen by running file `
tests/PCRE.R ` in the  R  sources (and perhaps installed).) People working
with PCRE and very long strings can adjust the maximum size of the JIT stack
by setting environment variable ` R_PCRE_JIT_STACK_MAXSIZE ` before JIT is
used to a value between ` 1 ` and ` 1000 ` in MB: the default is ` 64 ` .
(Then it would usually be wise to set the [ option
](/link/option?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` PCRE_limit_recursion ` .)

# Configuring Prettier with Visual Studio Code in Large Monorepos  

Working in a large monorepo brings unique challenges when it comes to consistent code formatting. Multiple applications, packages, and shared libraries often coexist, each potentially with its own configuration requirements. Prettier is a powerful and opinionated code formatter that can help enforce uniform style across such a codebase, but integrating it smoothly with Visual Studio Code (VS Code) in a monorepo requires careful setup.  

This guide walks through configuring Prettier for large monorepos, handling multiple project configurations, and enabling format-on-save behavior so developers can focus on building rather than formatting.  

---

## 1. Establish a Base Prettier Configuration  

In a monorepo, it’s best to maintain a **root-level Prettier configuration** that serves as the base for all projects. You can use a `.prettierrc` file or `prettier.config.js` at the repository root.  

Example `prettier.config.js`:  

```js
module.exports = {
  semi: true,
  singleQuote: true,
  trailingComma: 'all',
  printWidth: 100,
  tabWidth: 2,
};
```  

Placing this at the root ensures consistency, but individual projects can override settings if necessary.  

---

## 2. Handling Multiple Project Configurations  

In many monorepos, some projects have special formatting rules due to framework constraints or legacy code. Prettier supports **project-level overrides** by adding a `.prettierrc` file inside a specific project folder.  

For example, if a legacy application requires `semi: false`:  

```json
{
  "semi": false
}
```  

When VS Code runs Prettier in that folder, it will merge the root configuration with the project-specific overrides. This approach keeps most rules consistent while allowing flexibility.  

---

## 3. Installing Prettier in the Monorepo  

To avoid dependency conflicts, install Prettier once at the root:  

```bash
npm install --save-dev prettier
```  

If your monorepo uses workspaces (Yarn, npm, or pnpm), this ensures all projects share the same version, avoiding subtle formatting differences.  

---

## 4. Configuring VS Code to Use the Monorepo’s Prettier  

Open **Command Palette** → `Preferences: Open Settings (JSON)` and add:  

```json
{
  "editor.defaultFormatter": "esbenp.prettier-vscode",
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,
  "[javascript]": {
    "editor.defaultFormatter": "esbenp.prettier-vscode"
  },
  "[typescript]": {
    "editor.defaultFormatter": "esbenp.prettier-vscode"
  }
}
```  

This ensures VS Code uses the Prettier extension for formatting all relevant file types in the monorepo.  

---

## 5. Format-on-Save in Large Repositories  

When working in a large codebase, you want consistent formatting without manual intervention. VS Code’s `editor.formatOnSave` setting ensures every save triggers Prettier.  

For monorepos, you can also enable **code actions on save** to run Prettier alongside other tools:  

```json
"editor.codeActionsOnSave": {
  "source.fixAll": true
}
```  

This is particularly useful if ESLint or Stylelint are also in use, allowing all formatting and lint fixes to run automatically.  

---

## 6. Avoiding Conflicts Between Prettier and ESLint  

In monorepos, ESLint often overlaps with Prettier’s responsibilities. To prevent conflicts, install `eslint-config-prettier` and add it to your ESLint configuration’s `extends` array. This disables ESLint rules that conflict with Prettier formatting.  

Example:  

```json
{
  "extends": ["plugin:@typescript-eslint/recommended", "prettier"]
}
```  

This ensures ESLint focuses on code quality while Prettier handles formatting.  

---

## 7. Testing Your Configuration  

To verify that Prettier works across all projects:  

1. Open a file in each project.  
2. Introduce a style change that violates your Prettier rules (e.g., remove semicolons).  
3. Save the file and confirm VS Code reformats it according to the correct configuration.  

If certain folders don’t format correctly, check for `.prettierignore` files or conflicting extensions that override formatting behavior.  

---

## Conclusion  

In large monorepos, a well-structured Prettier setup with VS Code ensures consistent formatting across diverse projects. By maintaining a shared base configuration, supporting per-project overrides, and enabling format-on-save, teams can eliminate style debates and reduce friction during code reviews.  

With this configuration in place, developers can rely on Prettier to handle formatting automatically, keeping the focus on writing quality code and maintaining a smooth workflow across the entire repository.

               angles  degrees
    circle         -1      358

    >>> df.sub([1, 2], axis='columns')
               angles  degrees
    circle         -1      358

Multiply a dictionary by axis.

    
    
    >>> df.mul({'angles': 0, 'degrees': 2})
                angles  degrees
    circle           0      720
    triangle         0      360
    rectangle        0      720
    
    
    
    >>> df.mul({'circle': 0, 'triangle': 2, 'rectangle': 3}, axis='index')
                angles  degrees
    circle           0        0
    triangle         6      360
    rectangle       12     1080
    

Multiply a DataFrame of different shape with operator version.

    
    
    >>> other = pd.DataFrame({'angles': [0, 3, 4]},
    ...                      index=['circle', 'triangle', 'rectangle'])
    >>> other
               angles
    circle          0
    triangle        3
    rectangle       4
    
    
    
    >>> df * other
               angles  degrees
    circle          0      NaN
    triangle        9      NaN
    rectangle      16      NaN
    
    
    
    >>> df.mul(other, fill_value=0)
               angles  degrees
    circle          0      0.0
    triangle        9      0.0
    rectangle      16      0.0

#  torch.fmax  ¶

torch.  fmax  (  _ input  _ , _ other  _ , _ *  _ , _ out  =  None  _ )  →  [
Tensor  ](../tensors.html#torch.Tensor "torch.Tensor") ¶

    

Computes the element-wise maximum of ` input  ` and ` other  ` .

This is like [ ` torch.maximum()  ` ](torch.maximum.html#torch.maximum
"torch.maximum") except it handles NaNs differently: if exactly one of the two
elements being compared is a NaN then the non-NaN element is taken as the
maximum. Only if both elements are NaN is NaN propagated.

This function is a wrapper around C++’s ` std::fmax  ` and is similar to
NumPy’s ` fmax  ` function.

Supports [ broadcasting to a common shape
](../notes/broadcasting.html#broadcasting-semantics) , [ type promotion
](../tensor_attributes.html#type-promotion-doc) , and integer and floating-

# Understanding Date and Time Formatting Standards in Web Browsers

Working with dates and times in JavaScript can be deceptively complex. While the `Date` object offers a unified API across browsers, the way it interprets and formats input strings is influenced by international standards, localization settings, and subtle differences in browser engines. For developers building applications that rely on consistent date parsing, it is essential to understand these underlying behaviors.

## ISO 8601: The Common Ground

The most reliable format for date and time representation in JavaScript is the ISO 8601 standard, which outlines a clear, unambiguous syntax. A typical ISO 8601 date-time string looks like:

```
YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ
```

For example, `"2023-01-03T14:30:00Z"` represents January 3, 2023, at 14:30 UTC. The `Date` constructor in modern browsers can parse this format consistently, regardless of the user’s locale or regional settings. When possible, generating and consuming dates in ISO 8601 form minimizes discrepancies between environments.

## Localization and Regional Variations

Despite ISO 8601’s reliability, many applications must handle dates in localized formats. Browser implementations often rely on the operating system’s regional settings to interpret non-ISO date strings. This means that `"01-03-2023"` could be interpreted as January 3rd or March 1st, depending on whether the locale uses `MM-DD-YYYY` or `DD-MM-YYYY`.

Localization also affects formatted output. The `toLocaleDateString()` method allows developers to specify a locale and options for formatting:

```javascript
new Date().toLocaleDateString('en-US'); // "1/3/2023"
new Date().toLocaleDateString('en-GB'); // "03/01/2023"
```

By explicitly setting the locale, developers can ensure consistent presentation regardless of the user’s system settings.

## Timezone Adjustments

Web browsers internally represent `Date` objects as milliseconds since the Unix epoch (January 1, 1970 UTC). When displaying or parsing dates, browsers apply timezone offsets based on the user’s environment. This can lead to unexpected shifts when working with date-only strings or when crossing daylight saving time boundaries.

For example:

```javascript
new Date('2023-01-03').toString();
```

In most browsers, this will create a date at midnight UTC, which may appear as a different day if the local timezone is behind UTC. ISO 8601 strings with explicit timezone offsets (e.g., `"2023-01-03T00:00:00+05:30"`) help avoid these ambiguities.

## Browser Engine Differences

While modern browsers have largely standardized their date parsing behavior, subtle differences remain. Historically, Internet Explorer and older versions of Safari had inconsistencies when parsing non-ISO formats, sometimes defaulting to US-style month/day/year regardless of locale settings. Today, most engines—Chromium, Gecko (Firefox), and WebKit (Safari)—adhere closely to the ECMAScript specification, but developers should still test across browsers when dealing with varied input formats.

Additionally, the ECMAScript specification allows certain flexibility in parsing, meaning that non-standard formats may still be accepted but could behave differently in edge cases. For example, slashes (`/`) and dashes (`-`) are treated differently in some parsing scenarios, and two-digit years can be expanded differently depending on the browser.

## Best Practices for Consistency

To ensure predictable behavior across browsers:

1. **Prefer ISO 8601 input:** Generate dates in a standardized format from the source.
2. **Explicitly set locales for output:** Use `toLocaleDateString()` with a specified locale and options.
3. **Manage timezones deliberately:** Include timezone offsets when necessary, or use libraries that handle timezone conversions.
4. **Validate and normalize input:** Before parsing, detect and transform incoming strings into a standardized format.

Libraries such as Moment.js (legacy) or modern alternatives like Luxon and date-fns provide robust parsing and formatting utilities, abstracting away many browser-specific quirks.

## Conclusion

While JavaScript’s `Date` object offers flexible parsing and formatting capabilities, understanding the interplay between ISO standards, localization, timezone handling, and browser engine differences is key to building reliable date-handling logic. By adhering to standardized formats and explicitly managing presentation rules, developers can avoid the pitfalls of inconsistent parsing and ensure a seamless experience across diverse environments.

## Installation and usage After installing django-translated-fields in your Python environment all you have to do is define LANGUAGES in your settings and add translated fields to your models: ``` from django.db import models from django.utils.translation import gettext_lazy as _ from translated_fields import TranslatedField class Question(models.Model): question = TranslatedField( models.CharField(_("question"), max_length=200), ) answer = TranslatedField( models.CharField(_("answer"), max_length=200), ) def __str__(self): return self.question ``` ## Basic usage Model fields are automatically created from the field passed to TranslatedField, one field per language. For example, with LANGUAGES = \[("en","English"), ("de", "German"), ("fr", "French")\], the following list of fields would be created: question\_en, question\_de, question\_fr, answer\_en, answer\_de, and answer\_fr. This implies that when changing LANGUAGES you’ll have to run makemigrations and migrate too. No question or answer model field is actually created. The TranslatedField instance is a descriptor which by default acts as a property for the current language’s field: ``` from django.utils.translation import override question = Question( question_en="How are you?", question_de="Wie geht es Dir?", question_fr="Ça va?", ) # The default getter automatically returns the value # in the current language: with override("en"): assert question.question == "How are you?" with override("de"): assert question.question == "Wie geht es Dir?" # The default setter can also be used to set the value # in the current language: with override("fr"): question.question = "Comment vas-tu?" assert question.question_fr == "Comment vas-tu?" ``` TranslatedField has a fields attribute that returns a list of all the language fields created. ``` assert Question.answer.fields == ["answer_en", "answer_de", "answer_fr"] ``` question and answer can only be used with model instances, they do not exist in the database. If you want to use queryset methods which reference individual translated fields you have to use language-specific field names yourself. If you wanted to fetch only the english question and answer fields you could do this as follows: ``` questions = Question.objects.values_list("question_en", "answer_en") ``` Or better yet, using the to\_attribute helper which automatically uses the active language (if you don’t pass a specific language code as its second argument): ``` from django.utils.translation import override from translated_fields import to_attribute with override("en"): questions = Question.objects.values_list( to_attribute("question"), to_attribute("answer") ) ``` ## Changing field attributes per language It is sometimes useful to have slightly differing model fields per language, e.g. for making the primary language mandatory. This can be achieved by passing a dictionary with keyword arguments per language as the second positional argument to TranslatedField. For example, if you add a language to LANGUAGES when a site is already running, it might be useful to make the new language non-mandatory to simplify editing already existing data through Django’s administration interface. The following example adds blank=True to the spanish field: ``` from translated_fields import TranslatedField class Question(models.Model): question = TranslatedField( models.CharField(_("question"), max_length=200), {"es": {"blank": True}}, ) ``` ## Overriding attribute access (defaults, fallbacks) There are no default values or fallbacks, only a wrapped attribute access. The default attribute getter and setter functions simply return or set the field for the current language (as returned by django.utils.translation.get\_language). The default getter falls back to the first language of the field in case get\_language() returns None. Apart from that the default getter has no safetyfeatures and may raise an AttributeError and the setter might set an attribute on the model instance not related to a model field. Both getters and setters can be overridden by specifying your own attrgetter and attrsetter functions. If you want to always fallback to the default language and allow other languages’ fields to be empty you can use the TranslatedFieldWithFallback: ``` from translated_fields import TranslatedFieldWithFallback class Question(models.Model): question = TranslatedFieldWithFallback( models.CharField(_("question"), max_length=200), ) ``` What it does is: It adds a question field for all languages and automatically falls back to the first defined language if the current language’s field is left empty or if no language is activated at all. It also sets blank=True on all field instances except for the first. Since this is such a common use case the TranslatedFieldWithFallback can be used directly, or you can use the translated\_fields.utils.fallback\_to\_default attrgetter. A different use case might require falling back to any language, this is handled by the bundled translated\_fields.utils.fallback\_to\_any attrgetter. A different use case might be when you’re using locales with region codes such as fr-fr where you want to fall back to the language without a region code. An example attrgetter implementation follows: ``` from translated_fields import to_attribute def fallback_to_all_regions(name, field): def getter(self): value = getattr(self, to_attribute(name), None) if value: return value return getattr(self, to_attribute(name, get_language().split("-")[0])) return getter ```
